entries.body:
Orbit's deep-research process applies systematic-review methodology to structure how evidence is found, evaluated, synthesized, and reported. The frameworks below define how each phase is handled.

## Scope definition

Before searching, a review question must be bounded: Cochrane Ch. 2 [1] links question scope to stakeholder priorities, eligibility criteria, and a deliberate broad-versus-narrow choice. PICO framing (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) originates here and should be adapted where meaningful for software-research questions, but its health-intervention assumptions must be made explicit when transferred.

## Search planning and coverage

Cochrane Ch. 4 [2] prescribes broad term coverage within each concept, combining free-text and controlled vocabulary, and sourcing from multiple relevant source types to balance sensitivity against precision. Boolean and proximity syntax prescriptions in that chapter apply to database engines, not directly to semantic-search tools like Exa.

**PRESS checklist** [3] (2015 guideline) structures pre-execution search review across six concerns: research-question translation, Boolean operators, subject headings, text words, syntax/field tags, and limits/filters. Use it to audit a search strategy before scaling it across sources.

**PRISMA-S** [4] (Rethlefsen et al., 2021) is a 16-item extension to PRISMA specifically for reporting literature searches. It makes a search report inspectable and repeatable. Reporting completeness via PRISMA-S does not establish search completeness or study quality.

## Iterative searching strategies

**Berrypicking** (Bates, 1989) [5] treats a search as evolving rather than static: evidence found mid-search changes the next query, and information needs are refined incrementally across techniques and sources. No validated automated stopping rule exists in the original model.

**Relevance feedback and query expansion** (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, 2009) [6] distinguishes two reformulation modes: (a) global resources that expand vocabulary independent of results (thesauri, co-occurrence statistics), and (b) local relevance feedback and pseudo-relevance feedback that condition expansion on the current result set. Only the chapter introduction and contents were reviewed; claims about modern embedding retrieval are not supported by this source.

**Snowballing** (Wohlin, 2014) [7] gives a systematic procedure for expanding a literature set through backward (reference list) and forward (citing-document) traversal. It was demonstrated via replication of a published software-engineering review. Its conclusion that snowballing can substitute for database searching must not be generalised to universal completeness claims.

**TARCiS** (University of Basel, 2024) [8] provides consensus guidance on citation searching for evidence syntheses. It distinguishes citation direction (backward/forward), seed-reference selection, deduplication across indexes, and index coverage gaps. Standalone citation searching is explicitly unsuitable as a completeness-of-recall claim; it is a supplement, not a replacement.

## Bias assessment

**Cochrane Ch. 7** [9] separates three distinct judgments: risk of bias for each result, declared funding sources, and conflicts of interest. Applying it requires naming which domain of bias applies (e.g., selection, performance, detection) rather than collapsing everything into an opaque quality score. Designed for health interventions; adaptation to software research requires explicit mapping.

**Cochrane Ch. 13** (ROB-ME) [10] addresses the distinct problem of missing evidence in meta-analyses: it differentiates absence of study, unpublished result, and empty search result. ROB-ME is not a universal deception detector; it applies to pooled quantitative synthesis.

## Evidence certainty and GRADE

**Cochrane Ch. 14 / GRADE** [11] (Schünemann et al.) produces per-outcome certainty ratings using five downgrading factors: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. GRADE yields four levels (high, moderate, low, very low). These are not probabilities of truth or automated scores; each requires expert judgment. Use them to justify stated confidence limits, not to automate confidence assignment.

## PRISMA 2020 reporting

**PRISMA 2020** [12] (Page et al., 2021) supplies a 27-item checklist and flow diagrams for reporting systematic reviews. Key distinctions: *records* (database hits), *reports* (individual documents), and *studies* (distinct research units). PRISMA 2020 is explicitly a reporting guideline, not a conduct guide and not a methodological quality assessment tool. Applying selected PRISMA ideas to Orbit research does not constitute a full systematic review.

## Dataset and source documentation

**Datasheets for Datasets** (Gebru et al., arXiv:1803.09010) [13] proposes a documentation questionnaire covering composition, collection process, uses, and limitations for any corpus or dataset. It complements a simple source list by requiring explicit declarations before a dataset is used. A datasheet is declarative; domain shift and latent bias still require empirical verification.

**FAIR principles** (Wilkinson et al., 2016) [14] define four properties for scientific data and metadata: Findable (persistent identifiers, indexed metadata), Accessible (retrievable by identifier with open protocol, with defined access conditions), Interoperable (formal shared vocabularies), and Reusable (rich provenance, clear usage licence). FAIR applies to both data and metadata, not merely to file download. FAIR does not imply open, accurate, or freely reusable.

## Measurement uncertainty

**NIST TN 1297** (Taylor & Kuyatt, 1994) [15] defines Type A uncertainty (evaluated by statistical analysis of repeated measurements) and Type B uncertainty (evaluated from other means: prior data, specifications, expert judgment). It distinguishes these components from measurement error and from ground truth. The framework requires physical units and covariance assumptions; it is not an automated LLM confidence estimator, but its logic — naming the source and type of each uncertainty rather than conflating them — applies to research-claim documentation.

---

**Cross-cutting constraint**: All Cochrane and PRISMA sources were reviewed only via abstract, metadata, or chapter introduction extracts. Full checklist items and subsection procedures were not fully reviewed in Orbit's passes; consult the primary documents before claiming compliance with any specific item.

entries.body:
## Studio CLI Quickstart

Initialize a new Sanity project with the CLI [1]:

```bash
npm create sanity@latest -- --dataset production --template clean --typescript --output-path studio-hello-world
cd studio-hello-world
npm run dev
```

Also supported: `pnpm create sanity@latest`, `yarn create sanity@latest`, `bun create sanity@latest`. After `npm run dev`, open `http://localhost:3333` and log in with Google, GitHub, or email (same service used during CLI login) [1].

---

## Schema (`studio.config.js`)

The top-level `schema` key in `sanity.config.js` accepts `types` (array or callback) and `templates` (array or callback for initial-value templates) [2].

### Built-in field types (20)

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `array` | Arrays of other types |
| `block` | Rich text / block content editor |
| `boolean` | True/false |
| `cross-dataset-reference` | References across datasets |
| `date` | Date only |
| `datetime` | Exact date + time |
| `document` | Top-level document type |
| `email` | Email address |
| `file` | File upload |
| `geopoint` | Geographic coordinate |
| `image` | Image upload + editing |
| `number` | Numeric value |
| `object` | Custom nested object |
| `reference` | Hard reference to another document |
| `slug` | URL slug |
| `string` | Plain string or selectable list |
| `span` | Inline text span (used within block) |
| `text` | Multi-line plain text |
| `url` | URL |
| `globalDocumentReference` | Cross-workspace document reference |

### Common field properties

- `type` *(required)*: name of a valid schema type
- `name` *(required)*: field key in the data record
- `title`: human-readable label
- `description`: hint shown to editors
- `hidden`: `boolean | () => boolean` — hides the field conditionally
- `readOnly`: `boolean | () => boolean` — prevents editing conditionally
- `deprecated`: `{ reason: string }` — renders field read-only with a deprecation message; maps to `@deprecated` in GraphQL schema
- `options`: type-specific options object
- `validation`: `RuleBuilder` — see validation methods below [2]

### Validation rules

- `Rule.required()` — field must exist
- `Rule.skip()` — discards prior rules, makes field optional (rules after still apply)
- `Rule.either([rule, rule, ...])` — passes if any rule is truthy
- `Rule.all([rule, rule, ...])` — passes only if all rules are truthy
- `Rule.custom(value, context)` — custom function; return `true` to pass, or an error string [2]

### Schema organization

All types are registered under `schema.types` in `sanity.config.js`. Recommended: keep types in a separate `schemaTypes.js` file and import them [2].

Use `defineType`, `defineField`, and `defineArrayMember` helper functions for IDE auto-suggestions and TypeScript type-safety (optional) [2]:

```js
import { defineType, defineField, defineArrayMember } from 'sanity'
export const someDocumentType = defineType({
  name: 'exampleDocumentType',
  type: 'document',
  fields: [
    defineField({
      name: 'strings', type: 'array',
      of: [defineArrayMember({ type: 'string' })]
    })
  ]
})
```

Plugins may also contribute schema types via their own `schema.types` array [2].

---

## GROQ Query Language

GROQ (Graph-Relational Object Queries) lets you describe exactly what data your application needs, joining multiple document sets and shaping the response [3].

### Basic anatomy

```groq
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979] | order(releaseYear) { _id, title, releaseYear }[0...100]
```

- `*` — every document in the dataset
- `[filter]` — filter expression; all Sanity-system fields use `_` prefix (`_type`, `_id`, etc.)
- `| order(field asc|desc)` — sort; default direction is `asc`; pipe `|` is required before `order()`
- `{ fields }` — projection; shape the returned object
- `[0...100]` — slice (0–99); `[0]` returns a single item [3]

### Projections

A projection `{_id, title}` picks only named fields. You can also declare new fields:

```groq
*[_type == 'movie']{ "directorName": director->name }
```

**Naked projection**: append `.fieldName` to get a flat array of values instead of array-of-objects:

```groq
*[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title  // → ["Alien", "Blade Runner", …]
```

**Ellipsis operator `...`**: include all document fields *plus* computed ones. As of GROQ API `v2021-03-25`, order matters — the last property wins when there's a conflict. Best practice: put `...` first [3].

```groq
*[_type == "movie"]{ "actorCount": count(actors), ... }
```

### References and dereferencing

- Hard reference: `{ _ref: "document-id" }` — target cannot be deleted while referenced
- Weak reference: `{ _ref: "id", _weak: true }` — does not prevent deletion
- Dereference operator `->`: follows the reference and inlines the referenced document [3]

```groq
// Single reference
*[_type == 'movie']{ director->{ name } }

// Array of references — square brackets are mandatory
*[_type == 'movie']{ producers[]-> }
```

Omitting `[]` when expanding an array of references (`producers->` instead of `producers[]->`) returns a single null value — a common gotcha [3].

### Joins and parent operator

Use a sub-query in a projection to join data. The parent operator `^` references the outer document's scope:

```groq
*[_type == "person"]{
  _id, name,
  "movies": *[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title
}
```

`^._id` is the `_id` of the current person; without `^`, `_id` would resolve to the inner movie document [3].

### Filtering operators

| Operator/function | Example |
|---|---|
| Comparison | `releaseYear >= 1979` |
| Boolean | `&& \|\| !` |
| Text match | `title match "Alien*"` |
| Field presence | `defined(status)` |
| Array membership | `"sci-fi" in genres` |
| References filter | `references('ridley-scott')` |

### Pipe operator `|`

Required before pipe functions (`order()`, `score()`). Optional before projections. Valid only in those contexts [3].

```groq
*[_type == "project"]{
  "status": milestones | order(year desc)[0].status
}
```

### Array traversal in projections

Use `[]` to traverse arrays and apply projections or dereferences to each member:

```groq
*[_type == "movie"]{
  "images": images[]{ caption, "url": asset->url }
}
```

### Combining queries

A projection at the top level (no leading `*`) can combine multiple independent queries into one round trip:

```groq
{
  "mainStory": *[_id == "story-1234"],
  "topStories": *[_type == "story"] | order(publishAt desc)[0..10]
}
```

This is useful for loading all content needed for a page in a single cacheable request [3].

A schema describes the types of documents and fields editors may author in a Sanity Studio workspace.

Copy articleCopy article

The top level `schema` configuration accepts an object with two properties: `templates` and `types:`

- The `templates` property accepts an array of Initial Value Template configuration objects or a callback function returning the same.
- The `types` property accepts an array of schema definition objects or a callback function returning the same.

In both cases, the callback function is called with the current value as the first argument and a context object as the second. Thus, you can access schema definitions and Initial Value Templates implemented by plugins.

- ##### [templates](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#templates-3b7c7ccbff27 "Copy link to this section")



array \| function





An array of [initial value templates](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/initial-value-templates), or a callback function that resolves to the same.

- ##### [types](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#types-8137822cbda1 "Copy link to this section")



array \| function





An array of schema definitions or a callback function that resolves to the same.


The `templates` property is discussed in greater detail [in this article](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/initial-value-templates), and a reference article can be found [here](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/initial-value-templates-api). The rest of this article will deal with the default set of schema types supported in the Sanity Studio.

All schema types are listed below or in the documentation menu.

[**Array** \\
\\
Schema type for arrays of other types.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/array-type) [**Block** \\
\\
Schema type for block which provides a rich text editor for block content.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/block-type) [**Boolean** \\
\\
Schema type reference for expressing truthy values.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/boolean-type) [**Cross-dataset references** \\
\\
All you need to know about creating references across datasets.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/cross-dataset-references) [**Date** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Date type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/date-type) [**Datetime** \\
\\
The schema type for expressing an exact date and time.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/datetime-type) [**Document** \\
\\
Schema type reference for expressing documents.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/document-type) [**Email** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the email type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/email-type) [**File** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the File type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/file-type) [**Geopoint** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the geopoint type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/geopoint-type) [**Image** \\
\\
Schema type for uploading, selecting, and editing images.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/image-type) [**Number** \\
\\
Schema type reference for the Number type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/number-type) [**Object** \\
\\
Schema type to create custom types to use in a document.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/object-type) [**Reference** \\
\\
A schema type for referencing other documents.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/reference-type) [**Slug** \\
\\
A schema type for slugs is typically used to create unique URLs.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/slug-type) [**String** \\

\\
Schema type reference for the URL type.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/url-type) [**Global document reference** \\

[**Properties**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#k95998f28-7255-47eb-9def-7579c5688282 "Copy link to this section")

- ##### Required [type](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#type-798d15a99732 "Copy link to this section")



string





Name of any valid schema type _._ This will be the type of the value in the data record.

- ##### Required [name](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#name-6761a57a116e "Copy link to this section")



string





The field name. This will be the key in the data record.

- ##### [title](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#title-9bbaa7c16f19 "Copy link to this section")



string





Human readable label for the field.

- ##### [hidden](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#hidden-a6b799ef04e2 "Copy link to this section")



boolean \| () => boolean





Takes a static or a callback function that resolves to a boolean value and hides the given field based on it. You can use this property for conditional fields.

- ##### [readOnly](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#readonly-476941e109de "Copy link to this section")



boolean \| ()=>boolean





If set to `true`, this field will not be editable in the content studio. You can also return a callback function to use it as a conditional field.

- ##### [description](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#description-a91f4a01ca4e "Copy link to this section")



string





Short description to editors how the field is to be used.

- ##### [deprecated](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#deprecated-0a92c2f603c9 "Copy link to this section")



object





Marks a document type or a field as deprecated. This will render the field(s) as read-only with a visual deprecation message defined by the `reason` property.



Example: `deprecated: { reason: 'no longer used' }`



If you deploy a GraphQL API schema, this property will translated into the `@deprecated` directive.

- ##### [options](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#options-646e00663aba "Copy link to this section")



object





A unique set of options depending on the type. See the individual schema type references for available options.

- ##### [validation](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#validation-2fc0ab4b6082 "Copy link to this section")



RuleBuilder





Enables adding one or more validation rules to the field. See the [validation guide](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/validation) for more details, the section below for common validation methods, and the individual schema type references for additional methods.


[**Validation**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#a80ae6e5-1de7-4692-88f9-845a4a1678fc "Copy link to this section")

- ##### [required()](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#required-eda9af2f2c00 "Copy link to this section")





Ensures the field exists.



Example: `(Rule) => Rule.required()`

- ##### [skip()](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#skip-skip-rule-2543 "Copy link to this section")





Discards the validation rules set before it in the chain and makes the field optional. Rules chained after it still apply.

- ##### [either(\[rule, rule, ...\])](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#either-rule-rule-adcf41d09916 "Copy link to this section")





Accepts an array of rules. If any are truthy, the validation passes.



Example: `(rule) => rule.either([rule.required().min(1), rule.custom((_, context) => context.document?.category !== 'bicycle')])`

- ##### [all(\[rule, rule, ...\])](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#all-rule-rule-c914a2929e5a "Copy link to this section")





Accepts an array of multiple rules, all of which must be true for the validation to pass.



Example: `(rule) => rule.all([rule.required(), rule.custom((value, context) => { ... })])`

- ##### [custom(value, context)](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types\#custom-value-context-9fd616127457 "Copy link to this section")





Allows for custom validation rules. Receives the field value and the context. Must return true if validation passes, or an error message if validation fails.



Example: `rule => rule.custom(value => { ... })`


**Note**: The properties listed above are common for all data types. For a more thorough description of how to use them, see the individual schema type references.

[**Schema organization tips**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#k4d55bb107ed4 "Copy link to this section")

The studio loads all schemas defined under `schema.types` in `studio.config.js`.

```
//sanity.config.js
import {defineConfig} from 'sanity'

export default defineConfig({
  /* ... */
  schema: {
    types: [\
      {\
        title: "My Example Document Type",\
        name: "exampleDocumentType",\
        type: "document",\
        fields: [\
          {\
            title: "Greeting",\
            name: "greeting",\
            type: "string"\
          }\
        ]\
      }\
    ]
  }
})
```

To keep things organized, consider keeping the types array in a separate file and import it into `studio.config.js`.

```
//schemaTypes.js
export const schemaTypes = [\
  {\
    title: "My Example Document Type",\
    name: "exampleDocumentType",\
    type: "document",\
    fields: [\
      {\
        title: "Greeting",\
        name: "greeting",\
        type: "string"\
      }\
    ]\
  }\
]

//sanity.config.js
import {defineConfig} from 'sanity'
import {schemaTypes} from './schemaTypes'

export default defineConfig({
  /* ... */
  schema: {
    types: schemaTypes
  }
})
```

You should also consider using the [`defineType`](https://reference.sanity.io/sanity/index/defineType/), [`defineField`](https://reference.sanity.io/sanity/index/defineField/) and [`defineArrayMember`](https://reference.sanity.io/sanity/index/defineArrayMember/) helper functions when working with schemas. These will give you better IDE auto-suggestions and provide type-safety when used in TypeScript files. Using these functions is _completely optional._

```
import {defineType, defineField, defineArrayMember} from 'sanity'

export const someDocumentType = defineType({
  title: "Some Document Type",
  name: "exampleDocumentType",
  type: "document",
  fields: [\
    defineField({\
      title: "String array",\
      name: "strings",\
      type: "array",\
      of: [\
        defineArrayMember({ type: "string" })\
      ]\
    })\
  ]
})
```

[**Plugins**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/schema-types#k2e61273860da "Copy link to this section")

Plugins may also provide types. They will be available in the studio exactly like studio configured types.

Using plugins to organize your code can be helpful as the studio codebase grows.

The official [@sanity/presets](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@sanity/presets) package (currently experimental) is one example. It ships ready-made schema types for pages, links, images, SEO metadata, and rich text.

```
// pluginWithSchema.js
import {definePlugin, defineType, defineField} from 'sanity'

export const pluginWithSchema = definePlugin({
  name: 'plugin-with-schema',
  schema: {
    types: [\
      defineType({\
        title: "Plugin object",\
        name: "exampleObject",\
        type: "document",\
        fields: [\
          defineField({\
            title: "Title",\
            name: "title",\
            type: "string"\
          })\
        ]\
      })\
    ]
  }
})

//sanity.config.js
import {defineConfig} from 'sanity'
import {pluginWithSchema} from './pluginWithSchema'

export default defineConfig({
  /* ... */
  plugins: [pluginWithSchema()]
})
```

A tutorial on using the Sanity query language GROQ.

Copy articleCopy article

The idea behind our query language GROQ (Graph-Relational Object Queries) is to be able to describe exactly what information your application needs, potentially joining together information from several sets of documents, then stitching together a very specific response with only the exact fields you need.

If you need help setting up a client to perform these queries in your front end, you should check out the documentation for the client for [JavaScript](https://www.sanity.io/docs/libraries) or [PHP](https://www.sanity.io/docs/libraries). You can also check out the [GROQ Arcade](https://groq.dev/) if you want to query any JSON source and get familiar with the language.

[**Introduction**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k741625421a76 "Copy link to this section")

Let us start with the basics. We will take this simple query and pick it apart:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]
```

A query typically starts with `*`. This asterisk represents every document in your dataset. To do any useful work this is typically followed by a _filter_ in brackets. The filter above has two terms:

[**The filter**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#e9a260f5e979 "Copy link to this section")

First, we filter by document type. Every document in Sanity is required to have a type, and the type is always in the `_type` field. (We prefix any Sanity-specific fields with an underscore in an attempt to avoid clashing with any of _your_ field names.) So `_type == 'movie'` limits this query to documents of the type ‘movie’. `&&` is the operator “and”.

The second term `releaseYear >= 1979` assumes that the movies have a field called `releaseYear` that contains numbers. It will match any document where this number is larger than or equal to 1979.

[**Projections**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k727ecb6f5e15 "Copy link to this section")

So if we run this query, the result will be an array containing all movies from the year 1979 onwards in the dataset. Nice! However in a typical application movies might be huge documents containing information on actors, staff, posters, tag-lines, show-times, ratings, and whatnot. If our goal is to render a list of movies in an overview, we are wasting bandwidth. _Projections_ to the rescue.

The typical projection is wrapped in braces and describes the data we want to see for each movie. A nice and simple projection for this query would give us the id, title, and release year for each movie. It could look like this: `{_id, title, releaseYear}`. Putting it all together:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{ _id, title, releaseYear }
```

[**Basic sorting**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k935c175cf329 "Copy link to this section")

Now there is another problem. Our movies appear in some unspecified order. Let’s say we want to sort our movies by year. For this, we use the `order`-function. Order takes a number of fields and sort directions and orders your documents accordingly. We wanted to sort our movies by `releaseYear`. This is easily accomplished with `order(releaseYear)`, like this:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979] | order(releaseYear) {
  _id, title, releaseYear
}
```

_(We need the_`|` _operator here in front of the `order()`-function, we'll discuss that more later.)_

We think of GROQ statements as describing a data flow from left to right. First everything (`*`) flows through the filter` [_type == 'movie' && …]`, then all those movies flow through the `order()`-function which is then all mapped through the projection `{_id, title, ...}` which picks out the bits we want to be returned.

The order function accepts a list of fields, and optionally you can specify the sort direction for each field. If you wanted to sort the movies by year, and then within each year we want them alphabetical by title, we could use this ordering: `order(releaseYear, title)` And if we wanted the newest movies first, we could reverse the direction like this: `order(releaseYear desc, title)`.

#### Protip

`asc` means “ascending” and `desc` means descending in this context. If you leave out the sort-direction, Sanity will assume you want the ascending order.

[**Slicing the result set**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k16b34b599b2f "Copy link to this section")

This brings us to our final problem for this query: There are many movies in the world. Maybe our dataset contains tens of thousands. We need a way to describe which slice of that list we want to show. This is done using a _selector_. Let’s say we just wanted the first movie, we could add a `[0]` at the end. This works exactly like an array accessor and would return only the first element. If we want a slice, we can add [the range operator](https://www.sanity.io/docs/specifications/groq-operators) like this: `[0...100]`. This would return the first hundred movies from index 0 through 99. We can just as well ask for `[1023...1048]`or any other slice we desire. So there we are, our first basic query with filtering, ordering, projections, and selector:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979] | order(releaseYear) {
  _id, title, releaseYear
}[0...100]
```

[**References and joins**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#db43dfd18d7d "Copy link to this section")

A [reference](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/ids) in Sanity is a link from one document to another. Standard references are “hard” meaning when a document references another document, the target document _must_ exist, and is actually prevented from being deleted until the reference is removed. (There are also weak-references that do not "hold on to" the target. You make them by adding a `_weak`-key to the reference object like this: `{_ref: "<document-id>", _weak: true}`)

Let’s say we have “person”-type documents that looks something like this:

```
{
  _id: "ridley-scott",
  _type: "person",
  name: "Ridley Scott"
}
```

Keeping it simple, maybe our movies had a field `director` that contained a reference to a person. It could look something like this:

```
{
  _id: "alien",
  _type: "movie",
  title: "Alien",
  releaseYear: 1979,
  director: { _ref: "ridley-scott" }
}
```

Remember Sanity-specific fields are prefixed with an underscore, and an object containing a `_ref` key appearing anywhere in the document becomes a hard reference.

[**Expanding references**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k8ca3cefc3a31 "Copy link to this section")

Now we can do a number of useful things with this reference. The most basic thing is expanding the reference in place. Let’s revisit our movie queries from the introduction.

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear
}
```

Let’s say we wanted to include the director in the returned result. If we didn't know any better, we'd perhaps try something like this:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear,
  director
}
```

But if we just naïvely include the director in like this, we will just get whatever is in the director field on this document, which is the literal reference description:

```
[\
  {\
    _id: "alien",\
    title: "Alien",\
    releaseYear: "1979",\
    director: {\
      _ref: "ridley-scott"\
    }\
  },\
  … (more movies)\
]
```

This is not what we wanted, we wanted to follow that reference! By adding the dereferencing operator `->` we ask Sanity to follow the reference and replace it with the actual content of the document referenced:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear,
  director->
}
```

Now, this is useful. We’d get something like this:

```
[\
  {\
    _id: "alien",\
    title: "Alien",\
    releaseYear: "1979",\
    director: {\
      _id: "ridley-scott",\
      _type: "person",\
      name: "Ridley Scott"\
    }\
  },\
  … (more movies)\
]
```

Then maybe we didn’t want all that metadata with our director? We can add a separate projection for our director:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear,
  director->{name}
}
```

Our query now returns the director with just the name property we wanted:

```
{
  _id: "alien",
  title: "Alien",
  releaseYear: "1979",
  director: {
    name: "Ridley Scott"
  }
}
```

But we can do one better. We are not limited to the existing fields in the document in our projections, we can actually declare new fields. Let’s say we are building our compact movie list and we wanted just the title, year, and director name. We can get minimal cruft by extracting just the name and putting it in a new field, like this:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear,
  "directorName": director->name
}
```

Now our query returns exactly what we want in the form we want it:

```
{
  _id: "alien",
  title: "Alien",
  releaseYear: "1979",
  directorName: "Ridley Scott"
}
```

[**Expanding an array of references**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k584ed2426ff5 "Copy link to this section")

The example above shows how to expand a reference, but sometimes you'll be working with an _array_ of references. In the above example, let's say we wanted to add producers. Details on how to set this up in your schema can be found in the [Array](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/array-type#r7awwxtw) documentation, but we'll consider how you might query that data.

In this revised example, let's look at a query like this:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear, director,
  producers[]
}
```

We use square brackets after `producers` because it's an array. Note that we used `producers` with an `s`. The naming convention of your schema doesn't matter to GROQ (as long as you get the name right); it is our recommendation to [use the plural form for arrays](https://www.sanity.io/docs/apis-and-sdks/naming-things#k0c567e82634b).

Now, you might get this:

```
[\
  {\
    _id: "alien",\
    title: "Alien",\
    releaseYear: "1979",\
    director: {\
      _ref: "ridley-scott"\
    }\
    producers: [\
      {\
        _key: "<uniqueKey1>",\
        _type: "reference",\
        _ref: "gordon-carroll"\
      },\
      {\
        _key: "<uniqueKey2>",\
        _type: "reference",\
        _ref: "david-giler"\
      },\
      {\
        _key: "<uniqueKey3>",\
        _type: "reference",\
        _ref: "walter-hill"\
      },\
    ]\
  },\
  … (more movies)\
]
```

Like before, this isn't returning the details for each producer. We're getting references like we did at the beginning of the single reference example (and a `_key`, which [ensures uniqueness](https://www.sanity.io/docs/studio/array-type#k92296c6c45ea)). To expand references in an array, we will use the dereferencing operator (`->`) again. However, the square brackets are mandatory to traverse the array.

```
*[_type == 'movie' && releaseYear >= 1979]{
  _id, title, releaseYear, director,
  producers[]->
}
```

This will return the full details for each of the three producers referenced. Projections and [naked projections](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#dd66cae5ed8f) can be used just as with single references (the projection would go _after_ the dereference operator).

#### Gotcha

It would be easy to forget the square brackets when expanding an array of references (i.e., querying `producers->` instead of `producers[]->`, with the former returning a single null value). This is perhaps complicated by the fact that both `producers` and `producers[]` **_will_** return the array (albeit with unexpanded references). This is the nature of [how GROQ traversals work](https://sanity-io.github.io/GROQ/draft/#sec-Traversal-expression).

[**Filtering by references**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k7f12fe9f280b "Copy link to this section")

When dealing with references, we have a useful function called `references()` which can be used in filters to select only documents that reference specific other documents. Let’s say we want to list every movie Ridley Scott has been involved in. It looks like this:

```
*[_type == 'movie' && references('ridley-scott')]
```

[**Our first join**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k52023b22ca05 "Copy link to this section")

It is time to write our first proper join: Say we wanted to list people and include all the movies they were involved in? We’ll be querying the “person”-type documents, but in the projections for each person, we’ll ask for the movies they have been involved in. To do this we have to briefly cover the parent-operator `^`. Let’s look at the query first:

```
*[_type == "person"]{
  _id, name,
  "movies": *[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title
}
```

In a join, the parent operator is a way to reference the “parent” document. In this example the outer query for “person”-type documents fetches a bunch of people, and for each person, it returns the `_id` and `name`. Then we want to fetch the movies referencing that person.

Now we declare the new field “movies” where we start a new query for “movie”-type documents, but for each person, we want to limit our movie query to movies referencing that person. To achieve this we need the \_id of the person, but if we just wrote `_id` in the movies-query we’d reference the \_id of the movie.

To get to the fields of the person record we go “up” one level using the parent operator `^`. So `^` means the specific “person”-document that our movie query is about, and then `^._id` is the \_id of that person, just as `^.name` would be her name. So when we say `references(^._id)` in the query above, we limit our movies to movies referencing the current person.

[**Naked projections**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#dd66cae5ed8f "Copy link to this section")

There is one more new thing we haven’t talked about in this query. We could have written the movies-sub-query like this:

```
*[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)]{title}
```

Our list of movies would have looked something like this:

```
”movies”: [{title: “Alien”}, {title: “Blade Runner”}, …]
```

Since we just wanted the titles, we can use a [“naked projection”](https://www.sanity.io/docs/specifications/groq-syntax). By naming the field we want, like this:

```
*[_type == "movie" && references(^._id)].title
```

We get a nice, simple array of values, like this:

```
”movies”: [“Alien”, “Blade Runner”, …]
```

So, for completeness, the result of the full person w/movies query above could look something like this:

```
[\
  {\
    _id: "river-phoenix",\
    name: "River Phoenix",\
    movies: ["My Own Private Idaho", "Stand By Me", …]\
  },\
  {\
    _id: "ridley-scott",\
    name: "Ridley Scott",\
    movies: ["Alien", "Blade Runner", …]\
  },\
  …\
]
```

[**More ways to filter**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k99fd60e475f2 "Copy link to this section")

Sanity supports a growing number of ways to [filter your documents](https://www.sanity.io/docs/specifications/groq-operators). We have shown simple attribute comparisons with `_type == ‘movie’` and `releaseYear >= 1979`. We have shown filtering by references using the `references()`-function. In addition, we support:

- Text search using the match operator, e.g. `*[title match "Alien*"]`
- Filtering by the presence of a field, e.g. `*[defined(status)]` which only match documents that have the status property set to any value.
- The `in`-operator which matches values in arrays, as in `*["sci-fi" in genres]`, that matches all documents where `genres` is an array and that array contains the value `"sci-fi"`.
- You can of course combine these filters using the boolean operators `&&` (and), `||`(or), `!` (not), like this `*[_type == "movie" && (!("sci-fi" in genres) || releaseYear >= 1979)]`.

We are working on a full reference for the GROQ feature set. In the meantime, you'll find a comprehensive set of examples in the [cheat sheet](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/query-cheat-sheet).

[**Queries in projections**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/how-queries-work#k0fbcc468c3af "Copy link to this section")

A useful thing in GROQ is that filtering and [projections](https://www.sanity.io/docs/specifications/groq-syntax) also can be used inside your projections. Let’s say you work for an architect and every project has a number of milestones. A document might look something like this:

```
{
  _id: "timmerhuis"
  _type: "project",
  title: "Timmerhuis",
  milestones: [\
    {status: "competition", year: 2009},\
    {status: "design-development", year: 2011},\
    {status: "breaking-ground", year: 2013},\
    {status: "completed", year: 2015}\
  ]
}
```

And let’s say the view we are producing is about showing the current status of the project. We could achieve this by finding the latest milestone and extracting its status tag. This can be done in GROQ like this:

```
*[_type == "project"]{
  _id, title,
  "status": milestones|order(year desc)[0].status
}
```

Let’s pick apart the status query `milestones|order(year desc)[0].status` in some detail:

First, we take the field `milestones` which contain the (potentially unordered) list of milestones for the project. Using the pipe-operator `|` we send the contents of this array to the order function, which is instructed to sort the array by year in descending order `order(year desc)`. Then we take only the first element `[0]` (which is the latest milestone) and return the value of its `status` field. So now our project list would look something like this:

```
[\
  {\
    _id: "timmerhuis",\
    title: "Timmerhuis",\
    status: "completed"\
  },\
  …\
]
```

Let’s try another clever trick querying the contents of this object. Instead of a status field, we just want a boolean flag telling whether the project is completed. We could achieve this like this:

```
*[_type == "project"]{
  _id, title,
  "completed": count(milestones[status == 'completed']) > 0
}
```

Here we take the milestones, but select only the ones having the status “completed”. Then we `count()` the number of milestones matching this filter. If that count is `> 0` the result is `true`. So now our result would look something like this:

```

  {\

entries.body:
Sanity Context is a hosted, read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that gives AI agents structured access to your content — either from a live Sanity dataset (GROQ mode) or from a pre-built Knowledge Base index (Knowledge Base mode) [1]. Context MCP cannot write back to your dataset; for write tools, see the separate Sanity MCP server [1].

## Requirements

- **Context enabled for your organization.** An organization admin enables it from the Labs page (`https://sanity.io/manage/org/labs`) [1].
- **Organization API token with Context Viewer permissions.** Created under Manage > API > Tokens at the organization level (not a project read token). Viewer is the minimum; Editor also works [1].
- **An MCP-capable AI harness** (e.g. Vercel AI SDK or any MCP-speaking application) [1].
- **Knowledge Base mode additionally requires** at least one Knowledge Base that your token can read [1].

## Retrieval modes

Context serves content in two modes: GROQ mode queries the dataset at request time (suited to structured, schema-defined content); Knowledge Base mode serves a pre-built index (suited to answers spread across prose from multiple sources). The mode determines which tools the endpoint serves. For GROQ syntax details, see `sanity/groq_and_schema` [1].

Two URL query parameters switch an endpoint to Knowledge Base mode [2]:
- `mode=knowledge_base` — serves Knowledge Base tools instead of GROQ tools.
- `knowledgeBases=KNOWLEDGE_BASE_ID` — selects a Knowledge Base by its public id (begins with `kb`); separate multiple ids with commas.

For a deployed application, add the Knowledge Base as a source in the Context app instead of passing URL parameters. An endpoint whose sources are all Knowledge Bases serves Knowledge Base tools automatically [2].

## Knowledge Bases — concepts

A Knowledge Base is a pre-built index over material you choose (datasets, websites, uploaded files), belonging to an organization and able to draw from more than one project [3].

**Purpose:** Every Knowledge Base requires a purpose — one or two sentences describing its audience and job. The purpose steers the outline during a build (tagging entries `[core]`, `standard`, or `[peripheral]`) and is served to agents at the head of the outline [3].

**Outline:** A pre-generated index of every entry path with a one-line summary. Small enough for an agent to hold in context for an entire conversation. Agents use it to select the entries most likely to answer a question, then fetch those entries. Served via the `initial_context` MCP tool [3].

**Entries:** Markdown documents written from the Knowledge Base's sources, with citations back to originals. Entries belong to a build; they cannot be edited by hand. To change what a Knowledge Base says, update the source or add an instruction [3].

**Issues:** Detected when the same fact appears in multiple sources with conflicting values. The build raises a conflict rather than guessing. Coverage gaps, structural problems (missing topics, overgrown entries), and entry-removal proposals also surface as issues. Issues marked **Critical** affect facts an agent is likely to state [3][4].

**Instructions:** Standing decisions that carry across future builds. Resolving a conflict produces one automatically; you can also write instructions manually in the Instructions view. Each instruction is tied to one or more sources; when those sources change, the instruction is archived automatically [3].

## Creating a Knowledge Base

1. In the Sanity Dashboard, open **Context** and click **New knowledge base** [2].
2. Enter a **Title** and a **Purpose** (one or two sentences; the more specific, the better the outline) [2].
3. Click **Create knowledge base**, then **Add source** [2].
4. Click **Build entries**. Status reads **Entries up to date** when done. If build fails, remove failed sources and rebuild [2].
5. Review **Entries** (check topics and summaries) and **Issues** (start with Critical ones) [2].
6. Test through an agent with specific, verifiable questions [2].

Your organization's plan caps both the number of Knowledge Bases and the number of sources per Knowledge Base [2].

## Source types

A Knowledge Base requires at least one source and can combine all three types [5]:

**Dataset source**
- Documents selected by a complete GROQ query (e.g. `*[_type == "article"]{title, body}`). Bare filters are rejected [5].
- One dataset source per Knowledge Base; binds to one dataset. To switch datasets, remove and add a new source [5].
- Reads **published documents only**. A query matching nothing is rejected [5].
- Requires a role that can create datasets (Administrator or Developer by default) with unrestricted read access — a filtered read grant is not sufficient [5].
- Limit: **5,000 documents per dataset source** [5].

**Website source**
- Crawl starting from a URL. Respects `robots.txt`. Use the most specific URL possible [5].

**File source**
- Uploaded files **never re-sync**. To update, delete the import and upload the new version [5].

| Format | Maximum size |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | 500 MB |
| DOCX | 100 MB |
| PPTX | 100 MB |
| XLSX | 50 MB |
| HTML | 25 MB |
| PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF | 25 MB (images under 50 KB skip text extraction) |
| AsciiDoc | 25 MB |
| Markdown, plain text | Ingested directly |
| Source code, JSON, XML, CSV, TSV, YAML, and other plain-text | Ingested verbatim |
| ZIP, TAR, TAR.GZ | Expanded; each file ingested by its own format |

~40 additional text formats are also ingested verbatim. Files in unsupported formats are recorded with metadata but contents are not read. Every upload is capped at **5 GiB**; per-format limits apply first [5].

**When to upload vs. connect:** Connect as a dataset or website source for material that changes regularly. Upload for fixed material or content with no addressable source (e.g. a signed policy PDF) [5].

## Refresh schedule and maintenance

Dataset and website sources refresh on a schedule set in **Settings > Refresh interval**: **Weekly**, **Monthly**, or **Off**. New Knowledge Bases default to Weekly. Uploaded files never refresh [6].

A refresh does not automatically update entries: it recrawls sources, compares against the last build, and files issues. Entries change only when you apply those issues. While issues are open, the Knowledge Base sits in **Review** and serves entries from the last build [6].

- **Check for changes now:** Click **Check for changes** to run a refresh immediately [6].
- **After a refresh:** Agents receive refreshed content through the same outline; no agent-side change needed. If you have inlined initial context into a system prompt, refetch it after a rebuild [6].
- **Replace an uploaded file:** Delete the import and upload the new version [6].

**Refresh vs. full rebuild:**
- Refresh: files issues; applying them updates only affected entries.
- Full rebuild: reruns the whole pipeline over current sources, replaces the outline, rewrites every entry.

Rebuild when: **Rebuild required** callout appears; you changed the Knowledge Base's purpose; pipeline improvements are available; or the Knowledge Base has only uploaded files (no refresh path). Adding a new source does not need a rebuild — new material arrives as issues after upload [6].

To undo a bad build: in **Entries**, open an earlier outline version and select **Restore this version** to republish that build's entries (holds until the next build overwrites it) [6].

## Resolving issues

**Conflicts** show two claims side by side with their sources. Choose **Keep the current entry** or **Accept the incoming claim**, then click **Resolve issue**. When neither source is correct, fix the source material instead [4].

Resolution outcomes:
- "Entry is being updated now, and saved as an instruction for future rebuilds." — rewrite running as a background job.
- "Saved as an instruction that shapes your content on the next rebuild." — applies on next build [4].

**Suggested fixes** (add/remove/split/merge proposals): click **Apply**, **Dismiss**, or **Edit manually**. Issues that cannot be actioned in the app show "Manual action required" and offer only **Dismiss** and **Edit manually** [4].

**Dismissing:** Rejected without applying anything; safe to dismiss twice. Dismissed issues can be found in the dismissed filter and reopened. **Reopen and change your mind** clears the resolution and deletes the instruction it created [4].

You do not need to empty the issue queue before using a Knowledge Base. Prioritize issues marked **Critical** [4].

spans.quote:
#### Beta

Knowledge Bases are available as an opt-in beta feature. Features and limits may change before general availability. If you are on an Enterprise plan and need higher limits, talk to your Sanity representative.

A Knowledge Base belongs to an organization and can draw on sources from more than one project. Instead of reading and reconciling sources at query time, a build reads them ahead of time, resolves conflicts, and writes a set of entries an agent can retrieve from directly.

During a build, the purpose steers the outline. The tree of topics is designed against it, and it decides how central each entry is: subjects the purpose names come out tagged `[core]`, supporting material is standard, and content that merely arrived with the sources is tagged `[peripheral]`.

Agents read the purpose too. It heads the outline in initial context, right after the title, so it frames what the Knowledge Base is for before the agent chooses what to read.

[**The outline**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k030 "Copy link to this section")

The outline is the pre-generated index for a Knowledge Base. It contains every entry path and a one-line summary of what the entry covers. Entries that are more or less central to the purpose carry a `[core]` or `[peripheral]` tag.

Outline

```
## Acme product knowledge — Product specs, shipping, and support policies
4 entries.

products/latex/gloves [core]
  Glove grades, sizes, and what each is rated for
  topics: Grades, Sizing, Ratings

products/latex/industrial [peripheral]
  Industrial latex specs and tolerances

shipping/import-routes
  Customs paperwork and lead times by region
  related: support/returns

support/returns
  Return windows, exceptions, and who pays the freight
```

The outline is small enough for an agent to hold in context for an entire conversation. When a question arrives, the agent checks the outline, selects the entries most likely to contain the answer, and fetches those entries. Asked about return windows, it goes straight to `support/returns`.

Context MCP serves the outline through the `initial_context` tool, the orientation step at the start of a conversation. Every path in the outline is a readable entry; the hierarchy lives in the slash-delimited paths rather than in separate grouping rows. See [Context MCP tools](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-mcp-tools).

[**Entries**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k080 "Copy link to this section")

Each entry is a Markdown document written from the Knowledge Base's sources, with citations back to the original source.

Entries belong to a build. Every build can rewrite them, and they cannot be edited by hand. To change what a Knowledge Base says, update the source or add an instruction.

[**Issues**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k110 "Copy link to this section")

The same fact often appears in more than one place, and the copies drift. A help center says returns are accepted within 30 days; a product page says 45. Leaving the decision until query time asks the agent to reconcile the conflict every time someone asks.

A Knowledge Base detects conflicts during the build and raises an issue. The issue shows the claims side by side with where each came from, and you resolve it by choosing which claim is ground truth. Issues also flag structural problems: a topic the outline misses, an entry whose sources are gone, or one that has grown to cover two subjects. You apply those rather than resolving them. Coverage gaps are recorded but not surfaced for review. For how to work through the issues you can act on, see [Resolve Knowledge Base issues](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues).

[**Instructions**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k140 "Copy link to this section")

Instructions are standing decisions. Use them for anything Context should remember between builds, such as which source to trust when claims differ or how to describe a policy. Each instruction is tied to one or more sources, which is what lets a build retire it when those sources change. Resolving a conflict produces one.

You can also write instructions yourself in the **Instructions** view of the Context app: state the rule in plain language and choose the sources it anchors to. A rule shapes every entry that cites its sources, and it applies when those entries are next written, so rebuilding an entry from the outline applies a new rule right away. When you save a rule, Context checks the entries citing its sources and flags any that contradict it.

Building from Sanity data also gives you somewhere to apply corrections. When an issue comes from conflicting content, fix the content in the dataset. The next build inherits the correction, and an instruction the updated sources no longer support is archived automatically and surfaced for you to review.

[**What a build does**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k170 "Copy link to this section")

A build reads the sources, creates a tree of topics, writes each entry, and checks the result. Contradictions and structural problems surface as issues for you to review.

The tree follows what the sources are about rather than folder structure, URL paths, or file names. Three overlapping PDF manuals and a documentation site can become one set of topics. Each fact should have one home, and everything the sources cover should appear somewhere in the tree.

This work happens during the build. When an agent receives a question, the outline is ready and ambiguities have already been handled.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases#k210 "Copy link to this section")

- [Create a Knowledge Base](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base): build one from your sources and review the result.
- [Knowledge Base source types](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types): what datasets, websites, and files each accept.
- [Keep a Knowledge Base current](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base): refresh schedules and rebuilds.

[Previous **Inline initial context**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-initial-context) [Next **Knowledge Base source types**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types)

[**Dataset sources**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types#y020 "Copy link to this section")

Documents from a Sanity dataset, selected with a complete GROQ query such as `*[_type == "article"]`. Add a projection to control what each document carries, as in `*[_type == "article"]{title, body}`. The query has to select documents from the dataset, so a bare filter such as `_type == "article"` is rejected. Start with a narrow query; you can widen it later.

A Knowledge Base binds one dataset. To point at a different dataset, remove the dataset source and add a new one; the query itself stays editable. Website and file sources can be added repeatedly. A dataset source reads published documents only, and a query that matches nothing is rejected. Connecting one takes a role on the source project that can create datasets, which among the default roles means Administrator or Developer, plus unrestricted read access to the dataset itself. A role whose read grant is filtered to a subset of documents is not enough. One dataset source matches at most 5,000 documents, so narrow the query if you exceed that.

[**Website sources**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types#y040 "Copy link to this section")

A crawl starting from a URL. Crawls respect `robots.txt`. Use the most specific URL you can. A docs section is usually more useful than a whole domain.

[**File sources**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types#y060 "Copy link to this section")

Uploaded files never re-sync. To update one, delete the import and upload the new version; deleting an import removes every source it produced. Archives are expanded and their contents ingested individually, each by its own format.

A file source reads the formats below, subject to the size limits shown.

| Format | Maximum size |
| --- | --- |
| PDF | 500 MB |
| DOCX | 100 MB |
| PPTX | 100 MB |
| XLSX | 50 MB |
| HTML | 25 MB |
| PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF | 25 MB. Images under 50 KB skip text extraction. |
| AsciiDoc | 25 MB |
| Markdown, plain text | Ingested directly |
| Source code, JSON, XML, CSV, TSV, YAML, and other plain-text formats | Ingested verbatim |
| ZIP, TAR, and TAR.GZ archives | Expanded, then each file ingested by its own format |

Around forty further text formats are ingested verbatim in the same way, so the table is not the full list of what a file source reads. A file in a format with no handler is not rejected: it is recorded with its metadata, but its contents are not read. Every upload is capped at 5 GiB, and for the formats listed above the per-format limit applies first.

[**Choosing between connecting and uploading**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types#y090 "Copy link to this section")

If the material changes regularly, connect it as a dataset or website source rather than uploading a snapshot. Uploads are right for material that is fixed, or that has no addressable source, such as a signed policy PDF or an export from a system Context cannot reach.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types#y110 "Copy link to this section")

- [Create a Knowledge Base](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base). Add a source and run the first build.
- [Keep a Knowledge Base current](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base). Which sources refresh, and how often.

[**Prerequisites**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base#n020 "Copy link to this section")

- **Context enabled for your organization.** An organization admin can enable it from the [Labs page](https://www.sanity.io/manage/org/labs) of your organization in Manage.
- **Material to build from:** a website, files, or documents in a Sanity dataset. See [Knowledge Base source types](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types) for what each accepts.
- **Room on your plan:** your organization's plan caps how many Knowledge Bases it can hold. Creating one beyond that cap fails with a plan-limit error.

[**Title the Knowledge Base and write a purpose**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base#n050 "Copy link to this section")

The build is done when the status line reads **Entries up to date**. If it reads **Build failed** or reports that no sources could be processed, remove the failed sources or add new ones, then build again.

[**Review what the build produced**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base#n140 "Copy link to this section")

When the build finishes, open **Entries** to see the tree and what was written. Check that the topics you expected are present and that the summaries describe them accurately. **Issues** contains conflicts and other questions that need a decision. Start with the ones that could change important answers. See [Resolve Knowledge Base issues](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues).

![A screenshot of entries from a knowledge base, showing the entries structure and the contents of a single entry.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3do82whm/next/b485b4a7c6cea69177fd24fdd105d843abf00e0c-2776x1800.png?w=3840&q=75&fit=clip&auto=format)

Then test the Knowledge Base through an agent with questions people will actually ask. "What is the return window on bulk orders?" gives you something specific to check. "Tell me about Vandelay" does not.

[**Serve a Knowledge Base to an agent**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base#n170 "Copy link to this section")

Agents read Knowledge Bases through Context MCP. Two query parameters switch the endpoint to Knowledge Base mode:

- `mode=knowledge_base` serves Knowledge Base tools instead of GROQ tools.
- `knowledgeBases=KNOWLEDGE_BASE_ID` selects a Knowledge Base by its public id, which begins with `kb`. Separate several ids with commas.

For a deployed application, add the Knowledge Base as a source on the MCP in the Context app instead of passing these in the URL. An endpoint whose sources are all Knowledge Bases serves Knowledge Base tools automatically, and you can change what it serves without updating the agent configuration. An endpoint that also has a dataset source serves GROQ tools and ignores its Knowledge Base sources. See [Configure an MCP](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-configure-mcp).

The endpoint needs an organization API token with Context Viewer permissions, created under **Manage > API > Tokens** at the organization level, not a project read token. Test the connection with specific questions whose answers you already know.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base#n220 "Copy link to this section")

- [Keep a Knowledge Base current](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base). Refresh schedules, change detection, and rebuilds.
- [Knowledge Bases](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases). How the outline, entries, and instructions fit together.

[**Prerequisites**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v020 "Copy link to this section")

A Knowledge Base with at least one completed build. See [Create a Knowledge Base](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base).

[**Read a conflict and its sources**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v040 "Copy link to this section")

In the Context app in the Sanity Dashboard, open your Knowledge Base and select **Issues**. A conflict shows the two claims side by side, together with where each one came from. A help center saying returns are accepted within 30 days and a product page saying 45 is a typical example.

![A screenshot showing how a conflict is presented as an issue, and the options to resolve the conflict.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3do82whm/next/3f96dec5ef57d1698d2f95ec6197de3c7e0a28ed-1402x1092.png?w=3840&q=75&fit=clip&auto=format)

[**Choose which claim is correct**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v060 "Copy link to this section")

Select **Keep the current entry** or **Accept the incoming claim**, then click **Resolve issue**. A conflict has no third answer, so when neither source is right, correct the source material instead of resolving the issue.

The app then confirms which of two things happened. "The entry is being updated now, and saved as an instruction for future rebuilds." means a rewrite of the affected entry is already running as a background job. "Saved as an instruction that shapes your content on the next rebuild." means nothing changes until the next build. Either way, the instruction stands until the source material changes or you reopen the issue.

[**Apply a suggested fix**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v073 "Copy link to this section")

Only conflicts are resolved by picking a claim. An issue that proposes adding, removing, or splitting an entry carries one suggested fix instead, described as "Apply makes this change to your knowledge base." Click **Apply** to make it: a job rewrites the affected entries and commits a new revision. Click **Dismiss** to reject the proposal, or **Edit manually** to open the entry and change it yourself.

Not every issue kind can be actioned in the app. One that cannot shows "Manual action required. This issue type is not executable yet." and offers only **Dismiss** and **Edit manually**.

[**Dismiss or reopen an issue**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v076 "Copy link to this section")

Dismissing an issue rejects it without applying anything, and dismissing twice is safe. The confirm dialog reads "It won't be applied and moves to the dismissed list. You can still reopen the dismissed filter to find it later." Open a dismissed conflict and the resolution panel reads "This issue was dismissed, so no resolution will be applied." It cannot be resolved until it is reopened.

To undo a decision, click **Reopen and change your mind**. Reopening returns an accepted conflict to triage, clears its resolution, and deletes the instruction that resolution created.

[**Correct the source instead of resolving the issue**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v080 "Copy link to this section")

When the conflict comes from content you control, correcting the source is the more durable fix. Update the material and the next build inherits the correction. An instruction the updated material no longer supports is archived automatically, with a reason, and surfaced for you to delete or re-scope rather than removed silently.

[**Decide which issues to act on**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v100 "Copy link to this section")

You do not need to empty the queue before using a Knowledge Base. The queue holds conflicts, plus proposals to add, remove, split, or merge an entry. Issues of other kinds are not surfaced for review. Issues marked **Critical** affect a fact an agent is likely to state, so start there.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues#v120 "Copy link to this section")

- [Knowledge Bases](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases). How issues and instructions relate to entries and the outline.
- [Keep a Knowledge Base current](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base). Refresh schedules and rebuilds.

[**Prerequisites**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b020 "Copy link to this section")

A Knowledge Base with at least one completed build. See [Create a Knowledge Base](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base).

[**Set a refresh schedule**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b040 "Copy link to this section")

Website sources and connected datasets can refresh on a schedule. In **Settings**, set **Refresh interval** to **Weekly**, **Monthly**, or **Off**. New Knowledge Bases default to **Weekly**, and the setting saves as soon as you select it. The field appears only when the Knowledge Base has a website or a dataset source.

A refresh does not rewrite your entries. It recrawls the sources, compares them against the last build, and files issues describing what needs to change. Your entries change when you apply those issues, so a schedule on its own does not keep a Knowledge Base current. While issues are open, the Knowledge Base sits in **Review** and keeps serving the entries from the last build.

[**Respond to detected changes**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b060 "Copy link to this section")

When the material changes, the Knowledge Base overview shows **Changes detected**. Click it to see what changed in each source, or click **Check for changes** to run a refresh now instead of waiting for the next scheduled run. Applying the issues a refresh files keeps unchanged entries where they are: the outline changes only where the material has changed shape.

Agents receive refreshed content through the same outline, so no change is needed on the agent side. If you have inlined initial context into a system prompt, refetch it after a rebuild. See [Inline initial context into your system prompt](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-initial-context).

[**Replace an uploaded file**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b090 "Copy link to this section")

Uploaded files remain unchanged until you replace them. If a document is revised regularly, connect its source instead of uploading a snapshot so refreshes pick the change up on their own.

[**Decide between a refresh and a full rebuild**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b110 "Copy link to this section")

A refresh files issues; applying them updates only the entries the changed material affects. A full rebuild reruns the whole pipeline over the current sources and replaces the outline. Every entry is written again, so anything the previous build decided is reconsidered.

Rebuild when the Knowledge Base overview shows a **Rebuild required** callout, when you have changed the Knowledge Base's purpose, when the overview reports that pipeline improvements are available, or when the Knowledge Base has only uploaded files and so has no refresh path. A purpose change is the one case nothing else flags: the refresh compares sources only, so **Check for changes** reports nothing after you edit the purpose. Adding a source does not need a rebuild, since new material arrives as issues once the upload finishes ingesting.

A build you regret is not final. In **Entries**, open an earlier version of the outline and select **Restore this version** to republish that build's entries. The restore holds until the next build overwrites it, so use it to buy time while you fix the purpose, sources, or instructions that caused the bad build.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base#b130 "Copy link to this section")

- [Resolve Knowledge Base issues](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues). Handle the conflicts a refresh or a rebuild surfaces.
- [Knowledge Base source types](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types). Which sources can refresh and which cannot.

Sanity Context is a hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that gives AI agents structured, read-only access to your content. It serves your live dataset in GROQ mode, or material you have indexed ahead of time in Knowledge Base mode.

With Sanity Context, you can:

- **Answer questions from your own content.** Build assistants that respond from your documentation or help center rather than from a model's training data.
- **Recommend from your catalog.** Give a shopping assistant schema-aware access to products so it filters on real fields instead of guessing at them.

Build an index from your material and serve it to agents.](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-create-knowledge-base)

![Dark mode UI of a 'Context' application's overview page, displaying sections for 'MCP endpoints' and 'Knowledge bases' with lists of associated items and their statuses.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3do82whm/next/1ab1ef0b069bc1bbcebb78e50fe58b266f316dde-2450x1506.png?rect=0,0,2450,1501&w=3840&q=75&fit=clip&auto=format)

[**What Sanity Context provides, and what you bring**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#f2db5e857261 "Copy link to this section")

- **Context enabled for your organization.** An organization admin can enable it from the [Labs page](https://www.sanity.io/manage/org/labs) of your organization in Manage.
- **An organization API token with Context Viewer permissions.** Create it under Manage > API > Tokens at the organization level, and keep it server-side. Viewer is the least privilege that works; Editor also works.
- **A model and API key.** Simple schemas and questions work with small, fast models. If the agent picks the wrong tool or writes malformed GROQ, move to a more capable model.
- **Optionally, a frontend application to host the agent.** Next.js, for example.

GROQ mode additionally requires:

- **A Sanity project** with content.
- **Sanity Studio 5.1.0 or later** for server-side schema support.
- **A deployed schema.** Run `sanity schema deploy`, or open your hosted Studio once if you deploy with `sanity deploy`.

Knowledge Base mode additionally requires at least one Knowledge Base that your token can read.

[**Core concepts**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h240 "Copy link to this section") [**Retrieval modes**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h250 "Copy link to this section")

Context serves content in one of two modes. GROQ mode queries your dataset at request time and suits structured, consistent content the schema can point an agent at. Knowledge Base mode serves an index built ahead of time and suits answers spread across prose from several sources. The mode determines which tools the endpoint serves. See [Context retrieval modes](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-retrieval-modes).

[**Context MCPs**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h270 "Copy link to this section")

A Context MCP is the configuration an agent connects to: what content it can reach, and any instructions that shape its behavior. You create and manage MCPs in the Context app, so you can change what an endpoint serves without redeploying the agent. See [Configure an MCP](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-configure-mcp).

[**Initial context**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h290 "Copy link to this section")

At the start of a conversation the agent orients itself through initial context, which is mode-aware: a compressed schema overview in GROQ mode, or the Knowledge Base outline in Knowledge Base mode. If you control the system prompt you can fetch it over HTTP and skip the tool call. See [Inline initial context into your system prompt](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-initial-context).

[**Knowledge Bases**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h310 "Copy link to this section")

A Knowledge Base is a pre-built index over material you choose: datasets, websites, uploaded files. A build reads the material ahead of time, resolves conflicts between sources, and writes entries an agent can retrieve directly. See [Knowledge Bases](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-knowledge-bases) and [Knowledge Base source types](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-source-types). Once a Knowledge Base is live, you [keep it current](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-maintain-knowledge-base) and [resolve the issues a build raises](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-resolve-issues).

[**Content access**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h330 "Copy link to this section")

Access is decided when the agent connects: your organization token authorizes the connection, the MCP's sources decide what it serves, and a GROQ filter scopes dataset reads. Context MCP is read-only in both modes. See [Content access and security](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-security).

[**Limitations**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h350 "Copy link to this section")

- Context MCP is read-only. It cannot create or update documents.

- Knowledge Bases are an opt-in beta feature, and limits may change before general availability. If you are on an Enterprise plan and need higher limits, talk to your Sanity representative.

[**Next steps**](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context#h390 "Copy link to this section")

- [Quick start: connect an agent to Sanity Context](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-quick-start). The shortest path to something working.
- [Context MCP](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-mcp). The reference for endpoints, parameters, and configuration.
- [Context MCP tools](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-mcp-tools). Which tools an endpoint serves in each mode, and what each one does.
- [Sanity Context patterns and best practices](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-patterns). Scoping, routing, and instructing agents once the basics work.
- [Add insights to Sanity Context](https://www.sanity.io/docs/ai/sanity-context-insights). Track and analyze agent conversations.
