entries.body:
## OpenAlex Works API

OpenAlex indexes over 320 million scholarly works (journal articles, conference papers, books, book chapters, datasets, dissertations, preprints, and more), with tens of thousands added daily [1]. A work's OpenAlex ID takes the form `W2741809807`; fetch a single work at `api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807` [1].

Works are the central entity: authors, sources (venues), institutions, topics, funders, and citations all connect through them [1].

### Deduplication and identifier resolution

OpenAlex resolves multiple copies of the same work (preprint on arXiv, version of record in a journal, accepted manuscript in a repository) into one canonical record using two mechanisms [1]:

- **Persistent identifiers (PIDs):** a shared DOI, PubMed ID, or arXiv ID is treated as proof of identity and merges the location into the existing work.
- **Fuzzy metadata matching:** locations with no shared PID go through title normalization plus author-name matching; precision and recall are tuned over time.

A matched location enriches the existing work rather than creating a duplicate. Locations with neither a PID nor a usable title are dropped [1].

### Data sources

OpenAlex was seeded from the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG, discontinued 2021) and ingests primarily from Crossref (the open DOI-registration agency), plus DataCite, PubMed, HAL, and institutional/subject repositories [1].

### Linked metadata entities

Each work record connects to: authorships, locations, topics, keywords, funders, and awards [1]. Citations and FWCI live at a dedicated sub-resource; open-access status is separately documented.

### API capabilities

Base URL: `api.openalex.org/works`. Supports filter, search, sort, group, and paginate over work attributes [1].

---

## Crossref REST API

The Crossref REST API exposes scholarly metadata deposited by member publishers and trusted sources (including Retraction Watch) [2]. Metadata includes bibliographic fields, funding data, license information, post-publication updates, ORCID (author) IDs, and ROR (institution/funder) IDs [2].

**No sign-up is required.** Almost none of the metadata is subject to copyright; it may be used for any purpose. Some abstracts may be copyright-protected [2].

Base URL: `https://api.crossref.org/`. Results are returned in JSON [2].

### Quick-start examples

| Goal | Example request |
|---|---|
| Use the polite pool | `https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=0&mailto=yourmail@company.org` |
| Retrieve metadata for a DOI | `https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25` |
| Retrieve 10 records | `https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10` |
| Works in a journal by ISSN | `https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works` |

### Endpoints

| Endpoint | Returns |
|---|---|
| `/works` | List of registered content items (many filters available) |
| `/works/{doi}` | Single metadata record for a Crossref DOI |
| `/works/{doi}/agency` | Registration agency for a DOI (e.g., Crossref or DataCite) |
| `/journals` | List of journals with registered content |
| `/journals/{issn}/works` | Works in the specified journal |
| `/members` / `/members/{id}` | Crossref member organisations |
| `/members/{id}/works/` | Works associated with a member |
| `/prefixes/{prefix}/works` | Works under a DOI prefix |
| `/funders` / `/funders/{id}/works` | Open Funder Registry entries and linked works |
| `/types` / `/types/{id}/works` | Work types (e.g., `journal-article`, `monograph`, `grant`) |
| `/licenses` | Licenses used by registered content |

Full Swagger documentation at `https://api.crossref.org/` [2].

### Content negotiation

Single records can be returned in multiple formats via content negotiation; see the Crossref content negotiation documentation [2].

---

## Versioning, Corrections, and Retractions

Crossref's versioning best practices distinguish three version types: **preprint**, **version of record**, and **update notifications** (corrections, retractions, expressions of concern) [3]. Versions are linked rather than overwritten, preserving the original record's trace. The absence of a correction notice does not confirm a work is uncorrected — metadata depends on what publishers deposit [3].

**Practical implication for retrieval:** always check the `update-to` and `relation` fields in Crossref metadata and OpenAlex's `versions` context when assessing whether a retrieved work is the most current or has been retracted. Trusted sources like Retraction Watch feed into Crossref, surfacing post-publication updates [2].

---

## Research Integrity Metadata (Crossref + DataCite checklist)

The Crossref/DataCite integrity metadata guide (Amdekar et al., 2026-04) defines a checklist of metadata elements that connect actors and relationships beyond the DOI alone [4]:

- **Actors:** authors (with ORCID), affiliations (with ROR), funders (with funder IDs — now matched to ROR IDs when missing)
- **Relations:** linked datasets, software, preprints, and related identifiers
- **Rights and licensing:** license URIs, open-access status
- **Dates:** submission, acceptance, publication, update

Declared metadata may be incomplete or incorrect; the guide provides best-practice targets, not guarantees of data quality. Neither Crossref nor DataCite metadata constitutes peer-review quality assessment [4].

Starting in September 2026, Crossref began matching funder names deposited without identifiers to ROR IDs, improving funder-to-output linkage across the Research Nexus [2].

Eg: [W2741809807](https://openalex.org/works/W2741809807)Count: [327,124,722](https://openalex.org/works)Links:[authorships](https://help.openalex.org/data/authorships/), [locations](https://help.openalex.org/data/locations/), [topics](https://help.openalex.org/data/topics/), [keywords](https://help.openalex.org/data/keywords/), [funders](https://help.openalex.org/data/funders/), [awards](https://help.openalex.org/data/awards/)

A **work** is any scholarly document: a journal article, conference paper, book or book chapter, dataset, dissertation, preprint, and more. There are over 320 million works in OpenAlex, with tens of thousands added every day. A work’s OpenAlex ID looks like `W2741809807`; fetch one at [`api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807`](https://api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807).

Works are the central entity in OpenAlex — everything connects to them. [Authors](https://help.openalex.org/data/authors/) write works, [sources](https://help.openalex.org/data/sources/) publish them, [institutions](https://help.openalex.org/data/institutions/) get credit for them, [topics](https://help.openalex.org/data/topics/) describe them, and [funders](https://help.openalex.org/data/funders/) pay for them. Works also carry by far the most information of any entity: all twenty-ish entity types are first-class citizens, but works are the firstest class.

## About [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#about)

### Where works come from [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#where-works-come-from)

OpenAlex aggregates and builds on many open data sources. The catalog was seeded by the [Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Academic) — Microsoft Research’s effort to catalog the scholarly literature — whose final open dataset OpenAlex adopted when the project was discontinued in 2021. The other primary source is [Crossref](https://www.crossref.org/), the open DOI-registration agency. Alongside those, works are drawn from DataCite, PubMed, HAL, institutional and subject repositories, and more; see [How it’s built](https://help.openalex.org/data/how-its-built/) for the full ingest picture.

### How locations become works [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#how-locations-become-works)

OpenAlex starts from [locations](https://help.openalex.org/data/locations/): copies of a work hosted at particular places. A preprint on arXiv is one location; the same paper published in _Physical Review B_ is a second; the accepted manuscript in a university repository is a third. The job is to recognize that all three are one work. Two mechanisms do that, used together:

- **Persistent identifiers.** If a location carries a DOI, PubMed ID, or arXiv ID that OpenAlex already knows, it belongs to that work. This is the certain path: a shared PID is treated as proof.
- **Fuzzy metadata matching.** Locations with no shared PID — most repository copies, many preprints — go through a fuzzy matching algorithm built on title normalization plus author names, tuned over the years for precision and recall.

Whichever path matches, the location joins the existing work and _enriches_ it rather than minting a new one. If nothing matches, the location seeds a new work of its own; the only locations that don’t are ones with neither a PID nor a usable title, which are dropped.

Once a work exists, OpenAlex tracks its own metadata — title, abstract (and often full text), publication date, type — and the connections that make it useful at scale: authors, institutional affiliations, the source it appeared in, topics, funders, and citations.

How works cite each other — references, citation counts, and FWCI — has its own page: [Citations](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/citations/). How OpenAlex decides whether a work is free to read: [Open access](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/open-access/).

## In the API [Link to this section](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/\#in-the-api)

The Works endpoint is at [`api.openalex.org/works`](https://api.openalex.org/works). Fetch a single work by ID — [`/works/W2741809807`](https://api.openalex.org/works/W2741809807) — or a list, and [filter](https://help.openalex.org/api/filtering/), [search](https://help.openalex.org/api/searching/), [sort](https://help.openalex.org/api/sorting/), [group](https://help.openalex.org/api/grouping/), and [page](https://help.openalex.org/api/paging/) over the attributes documented on the [Attributes](https://help.openalex.org/data/works/attributes/) page. For the full list of endpoints see the [endpoints index](https://help.openalex.org/api/endpoints/).

Last updated September 18, 2026

[View as Markdown](https://help.openalex.org/data/works.md)

## REST API

[Metadata Retrieval](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/) [Access and authentication](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/rest-api/access-and-authentication/)

Our publicly available REST API exposes the scholarly metadata that members and trusted sources deposit with Crossref. This bibliographic metadata and much more—you will find funding data, license information, post-publication updates, ORCID and ROR IDs, and abstracts. You can search, facet, filter, or sample metadata from dozens of thousands of members from all around the world, and the results are returned in JSON format.

The metadata is deposited directly by our members, who publish the content represented by each metadata record. This is complemented by trusted sources, such as [Retraction Watch](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/retraction-watch/). You will also find other identifiers, such as ORCID for individuals, RORs for funders and affiliations, and more. In some cases we add these identifiers where they are missing in the original deposit. There is an overview of the available content at [Crossref stats](https://www.crossref.org/06members/53status.html).

No sign-up is required to use the REST API, and almost none of the metadata is subject to copyright, and you may use it for any purpose. Some abstracts contained in the metadata may be subject to copyright by publishers or authors.

## Quick start

Use [https://api.crossref.org/](https://api.crossref.org/) as your base URL. Add one of the available endpoints to query works, journals, members, funders, licences, prefixes, or types. Here are some examples to get you started:

| Retrieve metadata for a Crossref DOI | [https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25](https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25) |
| Retrieve records for 10 content items | [https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10](https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10) |
| Find works in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology, ISSN 03064530 | [https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works](https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works) |

entries.body:
Seven tools are catalogued here for converting PDFs and documents into structured, machine-readable text. All notes below are bounded Orbit research interpretations; consult official documentation or paper sources for exact version-specific behaviour.

## Docling (IBM Research AI4K, 2024)

Docling converts PDFs into typed JSON or Markdown via a modular pipeline that joins programmatic PDF tokens and coordinates, layout prediction, table structure recovery, and optional OCR, followed by final document assembly [1]. Code is MIT-licensed. Performance was sampled on 225 pages with OCR disabled; reported timings are not Orbit measurements and some speed/quality tradeoffs are backend-dependent [1].

## Nougat (Meta AI, ICLR 2024)

Nougat performs visual-to-markup conversion of scientific document pages, including mathematical expressions [3]. Training is predominantly English research papers. Known limitations (Section 5.5 of the paper): repetition loops, poor non-Latin-script behaviour, and page-level inconsistencies when pages are processed independently [3]. Inference speed depends on hardware and page text density.

## SmolDocling (IBM Research, ICCV 2025)

SmolDocling is a 256M-parameter vision-language model for end-to-end multi-modal document conversion [7]. It introduces **DocTags**, a unified output format that separates text from structural tags and includes spatial location information. DocTags supports nested captions, lists, and table structure [7]. Model performance is author-reported; deployment resource needs and production availability are unverified [7].

## GROBID

GROBID encodes scholarly-document sections, references, and annotations in a customised TEI XML schema [2]. Output is well-formed XML; schema validity is treated separately from well-formedness, and validation failures may indicate problematic extraction [2]. Well-formedness and schema validity do not establish semantic accuracy. The "latest" documentation page is unversioned and contains historical examples; exact deployed GROBID version is unverified [2].

## pypdf

pypdf extracts digitally encoded text from PDFs [4]. Key limitations:

- **Not OCR software**: cannot extract text from image-only or scanned pages, and cannot detect OCR mistakes [4].
- Absent semantic structure: reading order and table/column interpretation may be wrong or ambiguous [4].
- Complex coordinate handling and content-stream memory limits apply to layout mode [4].

Suitable for digitally born PDFs; requires pairing with an OCR tool for scanned content [4].

## OCRmyPDF

OCRmyPDF adds searchable OCR text layers to scanned or mixed-content PDFs while preserving source appearance where possible [5]. Uses Tesseract under the hood. Limitations:

- OCR can produce gibberish on low-quality scans [5].
- Tesseract does not supply paragraph or heading structure and can merge columns [5].
- Reading order may be incorrect [5].
- Ghostscript dependency: the v17 section states Ghostscript is no longer strictly required, while the final paragraph states it is required — this is an internally inconsistent dependency statement that must be resolved against a pinned version before adoption [5].

## PubTables-1M (Microsoft, CVPR 2022)

PubTables-1M is a dataset and modelling study addressing table detection, structure recognition, and functional analysis in unstructured documents [6]. Key concepts: oversegmentation is documented as a ground-truth ambiguity; headers and cells are canonicalized; annotations retain spatial locations and structural roles [6]. Trained and evaluated on a scientific-table corpus — success there does not establish correctness on arbitrary Orbit documents. Detection alone cannot validate cell values or header semantics [6].

## Summary comparison

| Tool | Primary output | OCR built-in | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Docling | JSON / Markdown | Optional | Speed/quality is backend-dependent |
| Nougat | Markup + math | Yes (visual) | Repetitions; English-dominant; page inconsistency |
| SmolDocling | DocTags (text + structure + location) | Yes (VLM) | 256M model; deployment unverified |
| GROBID | TEI XML | No | Validation ≠ semantic accuracy; unversioned docs |
| pypdf | Plain text | No | Cannot process scanned/image PDFs |
| OCRmyPDF | PDF with OCR layer | Yes (Tesseract) | No structural output; Ghostscript dependency ambiguous |
| PubTables-1M | Table annotations | No | Scientific-corpus scope; not a general parser |

entries.body:
Firecrawl provides three primary web data endpoints — `/scrape`, `/crawl`, and `/map` — all accessible via `POST` requests to `https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/`. SDK packages are available for Python (`firecrawl-py`) and Node (`firecrawl`). No API key is required to start; add one for higher rate limits [1].

---

## /scrape — Single-page extraction

`POST /v2/scrape` converts a URL into clean structured data. Auto-detects PDFs, DOCX, and other document types; pass a PDF URL the same way as any webpage [1].

### Output formats

Specify one or more in the `formats` array [1]:

| Format | Description |
|---|---|
| `markdown` | Clean markdown text |
| `summary` | Condensed summary |
| `html` | Cleaned HTML |
| `rawHtml` | Unmodified HTML as received |
| `rawBase64` | Base64-encoded raw HTTP response (must be the only format) |
| `screenshot` | Screenshot URL (expires after 24 hours); supports `fullPage`, `quality`, `viewport` |
| `links` | All links found on the page |
| `json` | LLM-extracted structured data (schema or prompt-based) |
| `images` | All image URLs |
| `branding` | Brand identity: colors, fonts, typography, spacing, UI components |
| `product` | Structured product: title, price, availability, variants (deterministic, no LLM call) |
| `audio` | MP3 from supported video URLs (e.g. YouTube); signed GCS URL, expires 1 hour |
| `video` | Best-quality video from supported URLs; signed GCS URL, expires 1 hour |
| `query` | Natural-language question answered from page content |

Use `product` for product pages (no schema needed, no LLM cost); use `json` for custom fields or non-product pages [1].

### JSON extraction

Pass `{ "type": "json", "schema": <JSON Schema> }` or `{ "type": "json", "prompt": "..." }` inside `formats`. Without a schema, the LLM determines the structure from the prompt alone [1].

### Credit costs for /scrape

- **Base**: 1 credit per page [1]
- **JSON mode**: +4 credits per page [1]
- **`question` / `highlights` formats**: +4 credits per page per format [1]
- **PII redaction**: +4 credits per page [1]
- **PDF parsing**: +1 credit per PDF page [1]
- **Audio or video extraction**: +4 credits per page [1]
- **Zero Data Retention (ZDR)**: +1 credit per page [2]
- **Cached results still cost 1 credit** — caching improves speed, not credit usage [2]

### Caching (`maxAge`)

Default freshness window is `maxAge = 172800000` ms (2 days) [2]:

- `maxAge: 0` — always fetch fresh (bypasses cache; slower, higher failure risk)
- `storeInCache: false` — do not store the result in cache
- `minAge: 1` — cache-only lookup; returns `404 SCRAPE_NO_CACHED_DATA` if no hit
- `changeTracking` — bypasses cache entirely; `maxAge` is ignored

Caching can speed up scrapes by up to 5x when fresh data is not required [2].

### Batch scraping

`POST /v2/batch/scrape` accepts a `urls` array. Returns a job ID for async polling, or blocks until complete with sync SDK methods. Batch scrape jobs expire after 24 hours [2].

### Location and language

Include a `location` object with `country` (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, default `US`) and `languages` (array, default matches country) [2].

### Zero Data Retention (ZDR)

Set `zeroDataRetention: true` in the request body. Firecrawl does not persist page content or extracted data beyond the request lifetime. Enterprise plan only. Screenshots are incompatible with ZDR — requests combining both return an error [2].

### Response status layers

Two separate status layers [1]:
1. **API status**: HTTP `200` + `success: true` = Firecrawl accepted and processed the request.
2. **Page status**: `data.metadata.statusCode` = HTTP status the target site returned (200, 404, 403, etc.).

---

## /crawl — Recursive site crawling

`POST /v2/crawl` submits a starting URL and recursively discovers and scrapes every reachable subpage. Handles sitemaps, JavaScript rendering, and rate limits automatically [3].

All `/scrape` options are available via `scrapeOptions` (JS) / `scrape_options` (Python) and apply to every page crawled [3].

### Credit costs for /crawl

- 1 credit per page crawled [3]
- JSON mode: +4 additional credits per page [3]
- PDF parsing: +1 credit per PDF page [3]

Before starting, Firecrawl checks remaining credits against the `limit`. Returns `402 (Payment Required)` if credits are insufficient [3].

### Configuration reference

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | (required) | Starting URL |
| `limit` | `10000` | Max pages to crawl |
| `maxDiscoveryDepth` | none | Max link-discovery hops from root; pages at max depth are scraped but links on them are not followed |
| `includePaths` | none | URL pathname regex patterns to include; at most 1000 patterns of 2000 chars each |
| `excludePaths` | none | URL pathname regex patterns to exclude; same limits as `includePaths` |
| `regexOnFullURL` | `false` | Match path patterns against full URL + query string instead of pathname only |
| `crawlEntireDomain` | `false` | Follow sibling/parent links, not just children of the start URL |
| `allowSubdomains` | `false` | Follow links to subdomains |
| `allowExternalLinks` | `false` | Follow off-domain links one hop; external homepage links are skipped |
| `sitemap` | `"include"` | `"include"` (sitemap + link discovery), `"skip"` (HTML links only), `"only"` (sitemap + start URL, no link discovery) |
| `ignoreQueryParameters` | `false` | Avoid re-scraping the same path with different query parameters |
| `ignoreRobotsTxt` | `false` | Enterprise only |
| `robotsUserAgent` | none | Custom User-Agent for robots.txt evaluation; Enterprise only |
| `delay` | none | Seconds between scrapes; forces concurrency to 1 |
| `maxConcurrency` | team limit | Max concurrent scrapes; defaults to your plan's concurrency limit |
| `webhook` | none | Webhook configuration for real-time notifications |
| `prompt` | none | Natural-language prompt to generate crawl options; explicit params override generated equivalents |

Path patterns use Rust regex (RE2-style). Look-around and backreferences are not supported. Invalid patterns return `400` [4].

### Polling and pagination

Submit returns a job ID. Poll `GET /v2/crawl/{id}` for status. Responses are capped at 10MB; when truncated, a `next` URL is provided for the next page of results. Terminal condition is the `status` field (`completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`) — do not use `next`'s absence as an exit condition on a failed/cancelled crawl [4].

`completed == total` on a finished crawl does **not** confirm every page succeeded — `total` excludes failed pages, so the counters converge regardless of failures. Retrieve failed pages via `GET /v2/crawl/{id}/errors`, which returns `errors` (network failures, timeouts) and `robotsBlocked` arrays [4].

Job results are available via API for **24 hours** after completion; after that, view in the activity logs [3].

### Result retrieval modes

- **`crawl` / `crawl` (sync SDK)**: blocks until completion, returns full results with automatic pagination.
- **`startCrawl` / `start_crawl` (async SDK)**: returns immediately with a job ID for manual polling.
- **WebSocket watcher**: `firecrawl.watcher(id, { kind: 'crawl' })` emits real-time events per page [3].

### Webhooks

Configure in the request body under `webhook`. Events [3]:

| Event | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `crawl.started` | Crawl begins |
| `crawl.page` | Each page is successfully scraped |
| `crawl.completed` | Crawl finishes |
| `crawl.failed` | Crawl encounters an error |

Every webhook request includes an `X-Firecrawl-Signature` header (HMAC-SHA256). Verify using your webhook secret from the Advanced tab of account settings [3].

### Non-determinism

Crawl results may vary between runs because pages are scraped concurrently and link-discovery order depends on network timing. To improve reproducibility: set `maxConcurrency: 1` (reduces interleaving but does not eliminate variation) or use `sitemap: "only"` if the site has a comprehensive sitemap [4].

---

## /map — Fast URL discovery

`POST /v2/map` returns most URLs on a website without scraping page content. Primarily discovers URLs from the site's sitemap, supplemented by SERP results and previously crawled pages [5].

**Cost: 1 credit per call**, regardless of the number of URLs returned (e.g. `limit: 100000` still costs 1 credit) [5].

### Parameters

- `limit`: max URLs to return
- `sitemap`: control sitemap inclusion behavior
- `search`: filter to URLs most relevant to a keyword; response ordered most-to-least relevant
- `location`: `{ country, languages }` for geo-targeted URL discovery (same ISO codes as /scrape)

### Response

Returns a `links` array of `{ url, title?, description? }` objects. Title and description are not always present [5].

### Tradeoffs vs /crawl

`/map` prioritizes speed over completeness — it may miss URLs not in the sitemap or cached data. For thorough recursive discovery with auditable error records, use `/crawl`. For links on a single specific page, request the `links` format from `/scrape` [5].

Firecrawl converts web pages into markdown, ideal for LLM applications.

- It manages complexities: proxies, caching, rate limits, js-blocked content
- Handles dynamic content: dynamic websites, js-rendered sites, PDFs, images
- Outputs clean markdown, structured data, screenshots or html.

For details, see the [Scrape Endpoint API Reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/scrape).

[**Try it in the Playground** \\
\\

-d '{
    "url": "https://firecrawl.dev",
    "formats": ["markdown", "html"]
  }'
```

```

# Scrape a URL and get markdown
firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev


# With multiple formats (returns JSON)
firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev --format markdown,html,links --pretty
```

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape\#caching-and-maxage)  Caching and maxAge\
\
To make requests faster, Firecrawl serves results from cache by default when a recent copy is available.\
\
- **Default freshness window**: `maxAge = 172800000` ms (2 days). If a cached page is newer than this, it’s returned instantly; otherwise, the page is scraped and then cached.\
- **Performance**: This can speed up scrapes by up to 5x when data doesn’t need to be ultra-fresh.\
- **Always fetch fresh**: Set `maxAge` to `0`. Note that this bypasses the cache entirely, so every request goes through the full scraping pipeline, meaning that the request will take longer to complete and is more likely to fail. Use a non-zero `maxAge` if freshness on every request is not critical.\
- **Avoid storing**: Set `storeInCache` to `false` if you don’t want Firecrawl to cache/store results for this request.\
- **Cache-only lookup**: Set `minAge` to perform a cache-only lookup without triggering a fresh scrape. The value is in milliseconds and specifies the minimum age the cached data must be. If no cached data is found, a `404` with error code `SCRAPE_NO_CACHED_DATA` is returned. Set `minAge` to `1` to accept any cached data regardless of age.\
- **Change tracking**: Requests that include `changeTracking` bypass the cache, so `maxAge` is ignored.\
- **Credits**: Cached results still cost 1 credit per page. Caching improves speed, not credit usage.\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#webhooks)  Webhooks\
\
You can configure webhooks to receive real-time notifications as your crawl progresses. This allows you to process pages as they are scraped instead of waiting for the entire crawl to complete.\
\

    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY' \\
    -d '{\
      "url": "https://docs.firecrawl.dev",\
      "limit": 100,\
      "webhook": {\
        "url": "https://your-domain.com/webhook",\

        },\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#event-types)  Event types\
\
| Event | Description |\
| --- | --- |\
| `crawl.started` | Fires when the crawl begins |\
| `crawl.page` | Fires for each page successfully scraped |\
| `crawl.completed` | Fires when the crawl finishes |\
| `crawl.failed` | Fires if the crawl encounters an error |\
\

  "success": true,\
  "type": "crawl.page",\

  "metadata": {}, // Your custom metadata\
  "error": null\
}\
```\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#verifying-webhook-signatures)  Verifying webhook signatures\
\
Every webhook request from Firecrawl includes an `X-Firecrawl-Signature` header containing an HMAC-SHA256 signature. Always verify this signature to ensure the webhook is authentic and has not been tampered with.\
\
1. Get your webhook secret from the [Advanced tab](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/settings?tab=advanced) of your account settings\
2. Extract the signature from the `X-Firecrawl-Signature` header\
3. Compute HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body using your secret\
4. Compare with the signature header using a timing-safe function\
\
Never process a webhook without verifying its signature first. The `X-Firecrawl-Signature` header contains the signature in the format: `sha256=abc123def456...`\
\
For complete implementation examples in JavaScript and Python, see the [Webhook Security documentation](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/webhooks/security). For comprehensive webhook documentation including detailed event payloads, payload structure, advanced configuration, and troubleshooting, see the [Webhooks documentation](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/webhooks/overview).\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#execution-and-result-accounting)  Execution and result accounting\
\
A crawl that finishes is not the same as a crawl that reached every page. This section describes what the crawl endpoints currently report about a run — the counters, the paging contract, the failure records, and the scope limits — so you can judge for yourself whether a run is complete enough to act on. None of these records is a guarantee of completeness.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#reading-the-status-counters)  Reading the status counters\
\
Every response from [Get Crawl Status](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get) (`GET /v2/crawl/{id}`) carries the counters that describe the run:\
\
| Field | Meaning |\
| --- | --- |\
| `status` | One of `scraping`, `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled` |\
| `total` | `completed` plus the pages still in flight: active, queued, and backlogged. **Failed pages are not counted.** |\
| `completed` | The number of pages that have been successfully crawled |\
| `creditsUsed` | Credits consumed by the crawl so far |\
| `createdAt` / `completedAt` / `duration` | Start time, finish time (terminal states only), and elapsed seconds |\
| `expiresAt` | When the results stop being retrievable from the API |\
| `next` | URL for the next 10MB page of results. Also emitted whenever `status` is not `completed` — see [Paging through results](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#paging-through-results). |\
\
`completed == total` on a finished crawl does **not** mean every discovered page succeeded. Because `total` sums completed, active, queued, and backlogged pages and excludes failed ones, a terminal crawl always has `active`, `queued`, and `backlog` at zero — so the two counters converge whether or not pages failed. The status counters cannot tell you that anything failed. Failed pages are enumerated only by [Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#failed-and-blocked-pages).\
\
The `data` array holds only pages Firecrawl successfully scraped. Pages that were attempted but never produced a result are not in `data` — read them from Get Crawl Errors, below.\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#important-details)  Important details\
\
By default, crawl ignores sublinks that are not children of the URL you provide. For example, `website.com/other-parent/blog-1` would not be returned if you crawled `website.com/blogs/`. Use the `crawlEntireDomain` parameter to include sibling and parent paths. To crawl subdomains like `blog.website.com` when crawling `website.com`, use the `allowSubdomains` parameter.\
\
- **Sitemap discovery**: By default, the crawler includes the website’s sitemap to discover URLs (`sitemap: "include"`). If you set `sitemap: "skip"`, only pages reachable through HTML links from the root URL are found. Assets like PDFs or deeply nested pages listed in the sitemap but not directly linked from HTML will be missed. For maximum coverage, keep the default setting.\
- **Credit usage**: Each page crawled costs 1 credit. JSON mode adds 4 credits per page, and PDF parsing costs 1 credit per PDF page.\
- **Result expiration**: Job results are available via the API for 24 hours after completion. After that, view results in the [activity logs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/logs).\
- **Crawl errors**: The `data` array contains pages Firecrawl successfully scraped. Use the [Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) endpoint to retrieve pages that failed due to network errors, timeouts, or robots.txt blocks.\
- **External links**: With `allowExternalLinks: true`, the crawler follows links pointing off your domain and scrapes each linked page once — it does not then crawl the links found on those external pages. Links to an external site’s **homepage** (a root URL with no path, e.g. `https://example.com/`) are intentionally skipped to avoid pulling in an entire unrelated site; these appear in [Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) with the code `EXTERNAL_LINK`. Redirects are followed to their destination — including a link that resolves to its canonical URL (for example `http → https` or the `www` variant) — so only redirects that land on an external homepage are skipped.\
- **Non-deterministic results**: Crawl results may vary between runs of the same configuration, because pages are scraped concurrently and link-discovery order depends on network timing. See [Execution and result accounting](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#execution-and-result-accounting) for what varies and how to make a run more reproducible.\
\
> Are you an AI agent that needs a Firecrawl API key? See [firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md](https://www.firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md) for automated onboarding instructions.\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#paging-through-results)  Paging through results\
\
Responses are capped at 10MB. When a response is truncated, `next` carries the URL for the following page of results.`next` is not purely a “more data remains” signal: it is also emitted whenever `status` is not `completed`, so a terminal `failed` or `cancelled` crawl can return a `next` URL even though no further results exist. Do not use the absence of `next` as your loop’s exit condition — on a failed or cancelled crawl it never disappears.The terminal condition is the status field. To read a run to the end:\
\
1. Poll `GET /v2/crawl/{id}` until `status` is one of `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`.\
2. While `next` is present **and** the last page returned a non-empty `data` array, follow `next` to collect the remaining results.\
3. Stop when `next` is absent, or when a page returns no new documents.\
\
The official SDKs handle this paging for you and return all results at once.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#failed-and-blocked-pages)  Failed and blocked pages\
\
[Get Crawl Errors](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-get-errors) (`GET /v2/crawl/{id}/errors`) records pages that did not make it into `data`. It returns two arrays:\
\
- `errors` — errored scrape jobs, each with `id`, `url`, `error` (the error message), and a `timestamp` of the failure. These are pages Firecrawl itself failed to scrape: network errors, timeouts, and similar. Links to an external site’s homepage that were intentionally skipped are reported here with an error code of `EXTERNAL_LINK`.\
- `robotsBlocked` — URLs that were attempted but blocked by the site’s robots.txt.\
\
This list is not guaranteed to be a complete enumeration of every failure: some internal failure classes are currently filtered out of `errors` before the response is built. Treat it as the record of failures Firecrawl reports, not as a proof that nothing else went wrong. The error code referenced above (`EXTERNAL_LINK`) is returned on error objects today but is not yet part of the published `GET /crawl/{id}/errors` schema; it is pending an API reference update.\
\
A page where the target site returned an HTTP error such as 404 is _not_ a crawl error: Firecrawl scraped it successfully, so it appears in `data` with the site’s status code in `metadata.statusCode`.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#what-the-crawler-is-scoped-to-reach)  What the crawler is scoped to reach\
\
Coverage is bounded by the scope parameters you set, all documented in the [configuration reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#configuration-reference) and the [Crawl endpoint reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/crawl-post):\
\
- **Children only by default.** Crawl ignores sublinks that are not children of the URL you provide. Use `crawlEntireDomain` for sibling and parent paths, `allowSubdomains` for subdomains, and `allowExternalLinks` to follow links off the domain.\
- **`includePaths` / `excludePaths` match the URL pathname**, as regex patterns — not the full URL, and not query parameters. Set `regexOnFullURL: true` to match against the full URL including query strings instead. The starting URL is also checked against `includePaths`: if it does not match, the crawl may return 0 pages.\
- **Path patterns are Rust regex (RE2-style) and are validated up front.** Look-around and backreferences are not supported, and a pattern that does not compile is rejected with a `400` instead of being silently ignored. Each field accepts at most 1000 patterns of at most 2000 characters each, and `includePaths` and `excludePaths` together may contain at most 1000 patterns and 100,000 characters. For keyword-style filtering, send one short pattern per term (`["pricing", "docs", "blog"]`) rather than combining terms into one long alternation.\
- **Sitemap mode.** With the default `sitemap: "include"`, URLs come from the sitemap plus recursive link discovery. `"skip"` uses HTML links only, so sitemap-only pages such as PDFs or deeply nested pages are missed. `"only"` crawls the sitemap plus the start URL and does not discover links from HTML.\
- **`maxDiscoveryDepth`** caps how many link-discovery hops from the root are followed. Pages at the maximum depth are still scraped, but links found on them are not followed.\
- **`limit`** caps the number of pages, and defaults to `10000`.\
- **`ignoreQueryParameters`** avoids re-scraping the same path with different query parameters.\
- **robots.txt is respected** unless `ignoreRobotsTxt` is enabled (Enterprise only).\
\
`maxConcurrency` defaults to your team’s concurrency limit, which is set by your plan — see [Rate limits](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/rate-limits).\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#when-results-vary-between-runs)  When results vary between runs\
\
Crawl results may vary between runs of the same configuration. Pages are scraped concurrently, so the order in which links are discovered depends on network timing and which pages finish loading first. This means different branches of a site may be explored to different extents near the depth boundary, especially at higher `maxDiscoveryDepth` values.To make a run more reproducible:\
\
- Set `maxConcurrency` to `1`. As the [configuration reference](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#configuration-reference) states, `maxConcurrency` is the “maximum concurrent scrapes” — it caps how many requests are in flight at once. That reduces timing-dependent interleaving, but it does not remove run-to-run variation: sitemap discovery is enqueued outside the cap, nested sitemaps are fetched as independent jobs, and the returned `data` array is ordered by finish time rather than discovery order. Setting `delay` also forces concurrency to 1.\
- Use `sitemap: "only"` if the site has a comprehensive sitemap, so the URL set comes from the sitemap rather than from link discovery.\
\

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#knowing-when-a-crawl-is-done)  Knowing when a crawl is done\
\
If you are not polling, the [webhook events](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#event-types) tell you the same thing: `crawl.page` fires for each page successfully scraped, and `crawl.completed` (or `crawl.failed`) fires when the run ends. Job results stay retrievable from the API for 24 hours after completion; after that, view them in the [activity logs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/app/logs).\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl\#configuration-reference)  Configuration reference\
\
The full set of parameters available when submitting a crawl job:\
\
| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |\
| --- | --- | --- | --- |\
| `url` | `string` | (required) | The starting URL to crawl from |\
| `limit` | `integer` | `10000` | Maximum number of pages to crawl |\
| `maxDiscoveryDepth` | `integer` | (none) | Maximum depth from the root URL based on link-discovery hops, not the number of `/` segments in the URL. Each time a new URL is found on a page, it is assigned a depth one higher than the page it was discovered on. The root site and sitemapped pages have a discovery depth of 0. Pages at the max depth are still scraped, but links on them are not followed. |\
| `includePaths` | `string[]` | (none) | URL pathname regex patterns to include. Only matching paths are crawled. At most 1000 patterns of 2000 characters each; see [scope](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#what-the-crawler-is-scoped-to-reach) for the combined limit and regex syntax. |\
| `excludePaths` | `string[]` | (none) | URL pathname regex patterns to exclude from the crawl. Same limits as `includePaths`. |\
| `regexOnFullURL` | `boolean` | `false` | Match `includePaths`/`excludePaths` against the full URL (including query parameters) instead of just the pathname |\
| `crawlEntireDomain` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow internal links to sibling or parent URLs, not just child paths |\
| `allowSubdomains` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow links to subdomains of the main domain |\
| `allowExternalLinks` | `boolean` | `false` | Follow links to external websites. External links are followed one hop (their own links are not crawled), and links pointing to an external site’s homepage are skipped — see [External links](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#external-links). |\
| `sitemap` | `string` | `"include"` | Sitemap handling: `"include"` (default), `"skip"`, or `"only"` |\
| `ignoreQueryParameters` | `boolean` | `false` | Avoid re-scraping the same path with different query parameters |\
| `ignoreRobotsTxt` | `boolean` | `false` | Ignore the website’s robots.txt rules. **Enterprise only** — contact [support@firecrawl.com](mailto:support@firecrawl.com) to enable. |\
| `robotsUserAgent` | `string` | (none) | Custom User-Agent string for robots.txt evaluation. When set, robots.txt is fetched with this User-Agent and rules are matched against it instead of the default. **Enterprise only** — contact [support@firecrawl.com](mailto:support@firecrawl.com) to enable. |\
| `delay` | `number` | (none) | Delay in seconds between scrapes to respect rate limits. Setting this forces concurrency to 1. |\
| `maxConcurrency` | `integer` | (none) | Maximum concurrent scrapes. Defaults to your team’s concurrency limit. |\
| `scrapeOptions` | `object` | (none) | Options applied to every scraped page (formats, proxy, caching, actions, etc.) |\
| `webhook` | `object` | (none) | Webhook configuration for real-time notifications |\
| `prompt` | `string` | (none) | Natural language prompt to generate crawl options. Explicitly set parameters override generated equivalents. |\
\

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#introducing-/map)  Introducing /map

The easiest way to go from a single url to a map of the entire website. This is extremely useful for:

- When you need to prompt the end-user to choose which links to scrape
- Need to quickly know the links on a website
- Need to scrape pages of a website that are related to a specific topic (use the `search` parameter)
- Only need to scrape specific pages of a website

[**Try it in the Playground** \\
\\
Test mapping in the interactive playground — no code required.](https://www.firecrawl.dev/playground?endpoint=map)

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#mapping)  Mapping

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#/map-endpoint)  /map endpoint

Used to map a URL and get urls of the website. This returns most links present on the website.URLs are primarily discovered from the website’s sitemap, supplemented with SERP (search engine) results and previously crawled pages to improve coverage. You can control sitemap behavior with the `sitemap` parameter.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#installation)  Installation

Python

Node

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#usage)  Usage

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#location-and-language)  Location and Language

Specify country and preferred languages to get relevant content based on your target location and language preferences, similar to the scrape endpoint.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#how-it-works)  How it works

When you specify the location settings, Firecrawl will use an appropriate proxy if available and emulate the corresponding language and timezone settings. By default, the location is set to ‘US’ if not specified.

### [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#usage-2)  Usage

To use the location and language settings, include the `location` object in your request body with the following properties:

- `country`: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (e.g., ‘US’, ‘AU’, ‘DE’, ‘JP’). Defaults to ‘US’.
- `languages`: An array of preferred languages and locales for the request in order of priority. Defaults to the language of the specified location.

Python

Node

cURL

```
from firecrawl import Firecrawl

firecrawl = Firecrawl(api_key="fc-YOUR-API-KEY")

res = firecrawl.map('https://example.com',
    location={
        'country': 'US',
        'languages': ['en']
    }
)

print(res)
```

const firecrawl = new Firecrawl({ apiKey: "fc-YOUR-API-KEY" });

const res = await firecrawl.map('https://example.com', {
  location: { country: 'US', languages: ['en'] },
});

console.log(res.metadata);
```

    "url": "https://example.com",
    "location": { "country": "US", "languages": ["en"] }
  }'
```

For more details about supported locations, refer to the [Proxies documentation](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/proxies).

## [​](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/map\#considerations)  Considerations

This endpoint prioritizes speed, so it may not capture all website links. It primarily relies on the website’s sitemap, supplemented by cached crawl data and search engine results. For a more thorough and up-to-date list of URLs, consider using the [/crawl](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl) endpoint instead.If you need more thorough recursive discovery with auditable result and error records rather than a fast approximation, use [/crawl](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl), which discovers pages by recursive link traversal as well as the sitemap and reports what it returned and what it failed to fetch — see [Execution and result accounting](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/crawl#execution-and-result-accounting). For the links on one specific page, request the [`links` format](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape#scrape-formats) from [/scrape](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape).

The Exa Contents API (`POST https://api.exa.ai/contents`) extracts clean page content from one or more known URLs or document IDs, handling JavaScript-rendered pages, PDFs, and complex layouts automatically [1]. Pass URLs in the `ids` field (also accepted as `urls` — the two are interchangeable) [1].

Contents features are also available on the `/search` endpoint for returned URLs at no extra charge up to 10 results per search ($1/1000 pages afterwards). For web search tool use cases, Exa recommends using Search + contents rather than `/contents` directly [1].

## Output shapes

Pick **one** content view per request. Requesting multiple views returns and bills each separately [1].

### Highlights
Returns relevant passages copied from the page. Best for agents, RAG, and factual lookups — keeps context smaller than full text.

```json
{ "ids": ["https://example.com/paper"], "highlights": { "query": "methodology and results" } }
```

An optional `query` parameter focuses extraction on the most relevant excerpts. See `search_apis/exa/search` for Dynamic Highlights guidance (sizing excerpts to relevance across multiple pages) [1].

### Full text
Returns the clean page body as markdown. Use when broad context, document structure, or details highlights might miss are needed. Cap size with `maxCharacters`:

```json
{ "ids": ["https://example.com/report"], "text": { "maxCharacters": 10000 } }
```

### Summary
Makes an LLM call for each page to produce a generated overview or extract structured fields. Pass a natural-language `query` for a prose summary, or a JSON Schema in `summary.schema` for structured extraction — the response is a JSON string matching the schema [1].

```json
{
  "ids": ["https://example.com/company"],
  "summary": {
    "schema": {
      "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
      "title": "Company Information",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": { "type": "string" },
        "industry": { "type": "string" },
        "foundedYear": { "type": "number" }
      },
      "required": ["name"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Content freshness (`maxAgeHours`)

Controls how fresh the extracted content must be [1]:

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Omit | Use cached content when available; fetch when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cache if newer than N hours, otherwise fetch |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh content |
| `-1` | Only use cached content |

Set `maxAgeHours` when stale content would be unusable (prices, availability, frequently updated pages). Pair with `livecrawlTimeout` (milliseconds, default 10000) to cap how long a fresh fetch may take; raise to 12000–15000 for slow sites [1].

The older `livecrawl` string parameter is deprecated. Equivalents [1]:

| Old `livecrawl` | Use instead |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0` |
| `"never"` | `maxAgeHours: -1` |
| `"fallback"` | Omit `maxAgeHours` |
| `"preferred"` | `maxAgeHours: 1` (approximate) |

Do not send `livecrawl` and `maxAgeHours` together [1].

## Subpage crawling

Set `subpages` (integer) to follow links from each starting URL. Use `subpageTarget` (array of strings) to prioritize particular site sections [1]:

```json
{
  "ids": ["https://docs.example.com"],
  "subpages": 10,
  "subpageTarget": ["api", "reference", "guides"],
  "highlights": true
}
```

## Images and favicons

Set `extras.imageLinks` to the number of image URLs wanted per page. Results also include a `favicon` and representative `image` URL when available. On `/search`, this sits at `contents.extras.imageLinks` [1].

## Common mistakes

`/contents` shares most options with `/search` but places them differently — there is no `contents` wrapper [1]:

| Instead of | Use |
|---|---|
| `contents: { text: ... }` | Top-level `text`, `highlights`, or `summary` |
| `useAutoprompt` | Remove — no query to rewrite on `/contents` |
| `stream: true` | Normal request — `/contents` does not support streaming |
| `numSentences`, `highlightsPerUrl` | `highlights: true`; use `highlights.maxCharacters` for a fixed limit |
| `tokensNum` | `text.maxCharacters` |
| `livecrawl: "always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0` |
| `crawledBeforeDate` | `snapshotAsOf` |
| `context: true` | `highlights` or `text`; build context from `results[]` |

The Python SDK uses snake_case throughout: `exa.get_contents(urls, highlights=True, max_age_hours=24)` [1].

Each response includes a `results` array with page metadata and content, a `statuses` array with per-URL success/failure info, and a `costDollars` object [1].

}
```

Pick one content view per request. Requesting highlights, text, and summary together returns and bills each view separately.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#content-freshness)  Content freshness

`maxAgeHours` controls how fresh the extracted page content must be.

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Omit | Use cached content when available and fetch the page when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cached content if it is newer than this many hours, otherwise fetch the page |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh content |
| `-1` | Only use cached content |

Most requests should omit this field. Set it when stale page content would be unusable, such as for prices, availability, or frequently updated pages. Pair a low `maxAgeHours` with `livecrawlTimeout` (milliseconds) to cap how long a fresh fetch may take.

Migrate from the deprecated livecrawl parameter

The `livecrawl` string parameter (`"always"`, `"preferred"`, `"fallback"`, `"never"`) is
deprecated in favor of `maxAgeHours`:

| Old `livecrawl` value | Equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| `"always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0` |
| `"never"` | `maxAgeHours: -1` |
| `"fallback"` | Omit `maxAgeHours` |
| `"preferred"` | No direct equivalent; use a low value such as `maxAgeHours: 1` |

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#crawl-subpages)  Crawl subpages

Set `subpages` to follow links from each starting URL. Add `subpageTarget` when you want Exa to prioritize particular site sections:

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.get_contents(
    ["https://docs.example.com"],
    subpages=10,
    subpage_target=["api", "reference", "guides"],
    highlights=True,
)
```

```
const result = await exa.getContents(
  ["https://docs.example.com"],
  {
    subpages: 10,
    subpageTarget: ["api", "reference", "guides"],
    highlights: true
  }
);
```

```
curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/contents" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "ids": ["https://docs.example.com"],
    "subpages": 10,
    "subpageTarget": ["api", "reference", "guides"],
    "highlights": true
  }'
```

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#images-and-favicons)  Images and favicons

Set `extras.imageLinks` to the number of image URLs you want from each page. Results also include
the site’s `favicon` and a representative `image` URL when available. On `/search`, this option
sits at `contents.extras.imageLinks`.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/contents/quickstart\#common-mistakes)  Common mistakes

`/contents` shares most of its options with `/search` but places them differently, and requests copied from older examples often carry parameters this endpoint never had. The [API reference](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/get-contents) is the source of truth for the current schema.

| Instead of | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `contents: { text: ... }` | Top-level `text`, `highlights`, and `summary`. Unlike `/search`, `/contents` has no `contents` wrapper. |
| `useAutoprompt` | Nothing. There is no query to rewrite on `/contents`; remove the field. |
| `stream: true` | A normal request. `/contents` does not support streaming. |
| `numSentences`, `highlightsPerUrl` | `highlights: true`. Exa sizes highlights to each page; set `highlights.maxCharacters` only for a fixed excerpt limit. |
| `tokensNum` | `text.maxCharacters`. |
| `livecrawl: "always"` | `maxAgeHours: 0`. Do not send `livecrawl` and `maxAgeHours` together. |
| `crawledBeforeDate` | `snapshotAsOf`. |
| `context: true` | `highlights` or `text`; build the context string from `results[]`. |

A few behaviors that are easy to miss:

- `urls` and `ids` are interchangeable. Pass either the page URLs or the `id` values from a search response.
- A fresh fetch (`maxAgeHours: 0` or a low value) waits up to `livecrawlTimeout` milliseconds (default 10000). Raise it to 12000–15000 for slow sites, or lower it when latency matters more than freshness.
- The Python SDK uses snake\_case for every key: `exa.get_contents(urls, highlights=True, max_age_hours=24)`.

entries.body:
Endpoint: `POST https://api.exa.ai/search`. Authentication via `x-api-key` header (or `Authorization: Bearer <key>`). The only required body field is `query` (string, minimum length 1) [1].

## Search types (`type`)

`type` defaults to `auto`. Choose based on latency vs. depth requirements [2]:

| Type | Use it when | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | Best default balance of quality and speed | ~1 second |
| `fast` | Latency-sensitive, user-facing search | ~450 ms |
| `instant` | Real-time path (autocomplete, voice) | ~250 ms |
| `deep-lite` | Lightweight research + synthesis, consistent latency | ~4 seconds |
| `deep` | Multi-step research + stronger synthesis | 4–15 seconds |
| `deep-reasoning` | Completeness and reasoning depth over latency | 12–40 seconds |

Deep modes run a research process rather than a single retrieval pass. For long-running research, list building, or multi-hop enrichment, prefer Exa Agent over `deep-reasoning` [2].

`additionalQueries` (array of 1–10 strings) adds query variations for broader coverage in deep-search variants; ignored for non-deep types [1].

## Writing queries

Write `query` in natural language. Include the subject, kind of source, and time period when relevant. `"Latest news on EU battery policy"` gives Exa enough intent; `"news"` does not. Do not use `site:` operators — use domain filters instead [2].

## Result count

`numResults` defaults to 10, maximum 100. Search does not support pagination. Contact sales (hello@exa.ai) to discuss limits above 100 [1][2].

## Filters

Filters are hard constraints; softer source preferences belong in the query text [2].

- **`includeDomains`** — restrict to listed sources. Accepts hostnames (`arxiv.org`), path prefixes (`anthropic.com/news`), and wildcard subdomains (`*.substack.com`). Max 1,200 entries [1][2].
- **`excludeDomains`** — remove listed sources. Same format as `includeDomains`, max 1,200 entries [1].
- **`startPublishedDate` / `endPublishedDate`** — ISO 8601 date-time; filter by publication date [1].
- **`category`** — focus on a content type. Known values: `company`, `publication`, `news`, `personal site`, `financial report`, `people`. `publication` surfaces scholarly papers with structured metadata (authors, venue, citations). `company` and `people` categories **do not support** `startPublishedDate`, `endPublishedDate`, or `excludeDomains`; using them returns a 400 error [1].
- **`userLocation`** — two-letter ISO country code (e.g. `"US"`) for localised results [1].

## Output shapes (`contents`)

Request at most one content view per result; requesting both highlights and text bills two views of the same page [2].

- **`highlights: true`** — excerpts most relevant to the query; recommended for most agent/LLM tasks. Exa selects the appropriate amount automatically. Pick this by default [2].
- **`text: { maxCharacters: N }`** — clean full-page markdown. Use when the task needs broader context or document structure. Limit both `numResults` and `maxCharacters` to control size [2].
- **`summary`** — LLM-generated summary per result. Adds a language model call for every result (see search_apis/exa/contents for full detail on content extraction from known URLs).

`contents.maxAgeHours` controls content freshness for the page extraction step, not result filtering by publication date [2]:

| Value | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Omit | Cached when available; fetch when needed |
| Positive integer | Use cache if newer than N hours; else fetch |
| `0` | Always fetch fresh |
| `-1` | Cache only |

## Output schema (`outputSchema`)

`outputSchema` synthesises search results into a single `output` object alongside the ranked `results`. Works with every search type; adds ~2 seconds of synthesis latency on top of the selected type [1][2].

- `type: "text"` with an optional `description` — generates freeform prose [2].
- `type: "object"` — generates structured JSON following JSON Schema. Supports up to 2 levels of nesting and 10 properties. Do **not** add citation or confidence fields; Exa returns them automatically in `output.grounding` [2].

`systemPrompt` (string) provides instructions for source preferences, deduplication, or other generation guidance. Use `systemPrompt` for behaviour and `outputSchema` for the response shape [2].

`stream: true` enables server-sent events for synthesis output; only active when `outputSchema` is provided [1].

## Compliance mode

`compliance: "hipaa"` enables enterprise HIPAA mode. This is an enterprise-only option that requires cache-only retrieval with supported parameters [1].

## Response structure

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `results[]` | Ranked list; each entry includes `title`, `url`, `publishedDate`, `author`, plus any requested `highlights`, `text`, `summary` |
| `output.content` | Synthesised value when `outputSchema` provided |
| `output.grounding[]` | Per-field citations and confidence from synthesis |
| `costDollars` | Estimated cost breakdown (billing computed from usage counters, not this object) |
| `searchTime` | Server-side processing time in ms; covers retrieval, may exclude synthesis |
| `requestId` | Unique request identifier for support |

`resolvedSearchType` and `context` response fields are deprecated; do not branch on them [1].

## Error codes

| HTTP | Tag | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `INVALID_REQUEST_BODY` | Missing or malformed field (e.g. missing `query`) |
| 401 | `INVALID_API_KEY` | Bad or missing API key |
| 402 | `DEFAULT_ERROR` | Payment / quota issue |
| 429 | `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | Rate limit hit |
| 500 | `DEFAULT_ERROR` | Internal error; retry |
| 503 | `SERVICE_OVERLOADED` | Capacity; retry with exponential backoff |

## Deprecated parameters

`includeText`, `excludeText`, `context`, `startCrawlDate`, `endCrawlDate` are deprecated and ignored or superseded. Use `highlights` or `text` instead of `context` [1].

The `query` field is the only required field when using the Search API.Write queries in natural language. Include the subject and, when useful, the kind of source and time period you want.Queries can be broad and exploratory. `"Latest news on EU battery policy"` gives Exa enough intent to discover relevant pages; `"news"` does not. When the source type matters, name it in the query:

```
Recent technical articles comparing hybrid and semantic retrieval for RAG systems
```

See [What’s in Exa’s Index](https://exa.ai/docs/search/data/overview) for what Exa’s index includes and how to search those content types.

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#search-types)  Choose a search type

`type` selects a search mode, each tuned for a different balance of speed, search depth, and synthesis. `auto` is the default and works for most searches.

| Type | Use it when | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | You want the best default balance of quality and speed | ~1 second |
| `fast` | The request is latency-sensitive | ~450 ms |
| `instant` | The request is on a real-time path such as autocomplete or voice | ~250 ms |
| `deep-lite` | The task needs lightweight research and synthesis | ~4 seconds |
| `deep` | The task requires multi-step search and stronger synthesis | 4–15 seconds |
| `deep-reasoning` | Completeness and reasoning depth matter more than latency | 12–40 seconds |

Latency figures are approximate and cover the search itself with cached content. `outputSchema` adds a synthesis step and a low `contents.maxAgeHours` adds a fresh page fetch; see [Budget latency and context](https://exa.ai/docs/search/best-practices#budget-latency-and-context).Deep modes run a research process rather than a single retrieval pass. See [Deep Search](https://exa.ai/docs/search/deep-search) for how that process works and how to use its additional controls.

Instead of `deep-reasoning`, use [Exa Agent](https://exa.ai/docs/agent/quickstart) for long-running research, list
building, and multi-hop enrichment. Agent has more compute per run and returns grounded,

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#output-shapes)  Output shapes

Every result includes metadata such as its title, URL, and publication date. Use `contents` to add highlights, full text, or a summary from the page.

- Highlights

- Full text


Highlights return the excerpts most relevant to your query. They give models and agents the
evidence they need without filling the context window with unrelated parts of each page.This is the recommended output shape for most tasks.Start with bare `highlights: true`. Exa uses the query to select an appropriate amount of
content from each result.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
    contents={"highlights": True},
)
```

```
const result = await exa.search(
  "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
  { contents: { highlights: true } }
);
```

```
curl -s -X POST "https://api.exa.ai/search" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "query": "How are inference providers reducing transformer latency?",
    "contents": { "highlights": true }
  }'

```

Pick one content view per request. Requesting both highlights and text returns and bills two views of the same page. `summary` is a third option, but it adds a language model call for every result.

`/search` and `/contents` accept the same content options in different places:

- **`/search`** nests `highlights`, `text`, and `summary` inside the `contents` object:
`"contents": { "highlights": true }`
- **`/contents`** has no `contents` wrapper. Its body is the content options themselves, so the
same fields sit at the top level next to `urls`: `"urls": [...], "highlights": true`

## [​](https://exa.ai/docs/search/quickstart\#output-schema)  Output schema

Add `outputSchema` when you want Exa to synthesize the search results. It works with every search type and adds an `output` object to the response.The ranked pages remain in `results`. The generated value is returned in `output.content`, with field-level sources and confidence in `output.grounding`.

- Freeform Text

- Structured JSON


Use `type: "text"` for generated prose. Add a `description` to specify its format or length.

Python

JavaScript

cURL

```
result = exa.search(
    "What changed in the latest EU battery policy?",
    output_schema={
        "type": "text",
        "description": "Summarize the changes in three concise bullets",
    },
)
```

```
const result = await exa.search(
  "What changed in the latest EU battery policy?",
  {
    outputSchema: {
      type: "text",
      description: "Summarize the changes in three concise bullets"
    }
  }
);

entries.body:
Gemini's Google Search grounding connects the model to real-time web content via the `google_search` tool, works with all available languages, and operates through the Interactions API (recommended) or the `generateContent` API [1].

## How it works

When `google_search` is enabled, the model handles the full pipeline automatically [1]:

1. Receives a user prompt with the `google_search` tool enabled.
2. Analyzes the prompt and decides whether a search would improve the answer.
3. Generates one or more search queries and executes them.
4. Processes search results and synthesizes a response.
5. Returns a grounded response with inline `annotations` (citations), plus `google_search_call` and `google_search_result` steps.

## Response structure

A grounded response is structured as a `steps` array. Key step types [2]:

- **`thought`** — model reasoning; includes a `summary` text block and a `signature`.
- **`google_search_call`** — contains `queries`: the actual search strings the model executed.
- **`google_search_result`** — contains `search_suggestions`, an HTML snippet for rendering search suggestions in your UI. Full usage requirements are in the Terms of Service.
- **`model_output`** — the synthesized answer. Its `content` array holds `text` blocks with `annotations`.

### `url_citation` annotation fields

Each `url_citation` annotation on a `text` block provides [2]:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | `"url_citation"` |
| `url` | Source URL |
| `title` | Domain label (e.g., `"aljazeera.com"`) |
| `start_index` | Character offset in the text where the cited segment begins |
| `end_index` | Character offset where the cited segment ends |

Use `text[start_index:end_index]` (Python) or `text.slice(startIndex, endIndex)` (JS) to extract the exact cited span [3].

## Inline citation extraction (Python example)

```python
for step in interaction.steps:
    if step.type == "model_output":
        for content_block in step.content:
            if content_block.type == "text":
                print(content_block.text)
                if content_block.annotations:
                    for annotation in content_block.annotations:
                        if annotation.type == "url_citation":
                            cited_text = content_block.text[annotation.start_index:annotation.end_index]
                            print(f"  [{annotation.title}]({annotation.url})")
                            print(f'    Cited text: "{cited_text}"')
```
[3]

## Pricing

Billing differs by model generation [3]:

- **Gemini 3 models:** billed **per search query** the model executes. If the model runs multiple queries for one prompt, each counts as a separate billable use. Empty web search queries are excluded from the count.
- **Gemini 2.5 and older models:** billed **per prompt**.

For exact rates, see the Gemini API pricing page.

## Supported tool combinations

Google Search grounding can be combined with [3]:

- **Code execution**
- **URL context** (to additionally ground responses in specific URLs you provide)
- **Grounding with Google Maps** (Gemini 3.5 Flash and later)
- **Custom tools / function calling** (Gemini 3 models only)

## Pricing

When you use Grounding with Google Search with Gemini 3, your project is billed
for each search query that the model decides to execute. If the model decides to
execute multiple search queries to answer a single prompt (for example,
searching for `"UEFA Euro 2024 winner"` and `"Spain vs England Euro 2024 final
score"` within the same API call), this counts as two billable uses of the tool
for that request. For billing purposes, we ignore the empty web search queries
when counting unique queries. This billing model only applies to Gemini 3
models; when you use search grounding with Gemini 2.5 or older models, your
project is billed per prompt.

For detailed pricing information, see the [Gemini API pricing\\
page](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing).

## Understanding the grounding response

When a response is successfully grounded, the model's text output includes
inline `annotations` directly on the text content block. These annotations
provide citation information linking parts of the response to their sources.

```
{
  "steps": [\
    {\
      "type": "thought",\
      "summary": [\
        {\
          "type": "text",\
          "text": "The user is asking for the winner of Euro 2024. I need to search for the result of the Euro 2024 final."\
        }\
      ],\
      "signature": "CoMDAXLI2nynRYojJIy6B1Jh9os2crpWLfB0..."\
    },\
    {\
      "type": "google_search_call",\
      "arguments": {\
        "queries": ["UEFA Euro 2024 winner"]\
      }\
    },\
    {\
      "type": "google_search_result",\
      "call_id": "search_001",\
      "result": [\
        {\
          "search_suggestions": "<!-- HTML and CSS for the search widget -->"\
        }\
      ]\
    },\
    {\
      "type": "model_output",\
      "content": [\
        {\
          "type": "text",\
          "text": "Spain won Euro 2024, defeating England 2-1 in the final. This victory marks Spain's record fourth European Championship title.",\
          "annotations": [\
            {\
              "type": "url_citation",\
              "url": "https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/euro-2024-final",\
              "title": "aljazeera.com",\
              "start_index": 0,\
              "end_index": 56\
            },\
            {\
              "type": "url_citation",\
              "url": "https://www.uefa.com/euro2024/news/spain-wins-euro-2024",\
              "title": "uefa.com",\
              "start_index": 57,\
              "end_index": 124\
            }\
          ]\
        }\
      ]\
    }\
  ]
}
```

The key fields in the response:

- `google_search_call` : Contains the search `queries` the model executed.
- `google_search_result` : Contains `search_suggestions`, an HTML snippet
for rendering search suggestions in your UI. Full usage requirements are
detailed in the [Terms of Service](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms#grounding-with-google-search).
- `text` with `annotations` : The model's synthesized answer with inline
citations. Each `url_citation` annotation links a text segment (defined
by `start_index` and `end_index`) to a source URL. This is the key to
building inline citations.

Grounding with Google Search can also be used in combination with the [URL\\
context tool](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/url-context) to ground responses in
both public web data and the specific URLs you provide.
